items.stem: A contractor needs a new Linux account for a six-month engagement. An administrator must create it, confirm the UID the system assigned it, and be ready to remove it entirely once the contract ends. Which sequence of commands does this?

options.text: `useradd` to create the account, `id` to confirm the UID it was assigned, and `userdel` to remove it once the engagement ends
options.why: Each command matches the stage it is used at: creation, confirmation, and eventual removal of the account.

options.text: Starting from `usermod`, on the belief that it can both create a fresh account and later adjust it, then finishing with `id` and `userdel`
options.why: A common slip: `usermod` only changes an account that already exists, so nothing is created by reaching for it first.

options.text: The same `useradd` and `userdel` pair, but checking the assigned UID with `whoami` in between
options.why: `whoami` reports the identity of whoever is running the command, not the UID of the account just created.

options.text: Managing the whole lifecycle with `groupadd` and `groupdel` instead, still checking the UID with `id`
options.why: That pair manages a group, not a user account, so nothing about the contractor's login is created at all.

items.rationale: A named identity is created with `useradd`, its assigned UID is confirmed with `id`, and it is removed with `userdel` once no longer needed. `usermod` changes an existing account rather than creating one, and `whoami` reports the caller rather than a named account.

items.stem: A new hire needs to read and write files shared by the `developers` team without gaining a separate login of their own. Which two concepts does the fix combine?

options.text: A group named `developers`, granting the permission once, and the user account being added as a member of it
options.why: A group lets a permission be granted once and shared by every member, which is exactly the shared-folder scenario.

options.text: A second user account named `developers`, sharing its UID with every team member
options.why: A user account is one named identity with one UID; it is not how membership in a team is modelled.

options.text: A service account created for the `developers` team so nobody needs an interactive login
options.why: A service account exists to run a daemon, not to give a person shared access to files.

options.text: A `sudoers` rule granting the new hire root on the shared files — root access is far broader than the stated need and bypasses the ordinary permission model rather than using it
options.why: Root access is far broader than the stated need and bypasses the ordinary permission model rather than using it.

items.rationale: A group is a named collection of users used to grant a permission once to many accounts, so the resolution is a `developers` group with the new account added as a member, rather than a new personal account or blanket root access. Membership can be confirmed afterward with `groups`.

items.stem: An administrator needs to create a `deploy` group, remove an old `contractors` group that is no longer needed, and add an existing user to `deploy` without disturbing any group memberships that user already has. Which three commands do this?

options.text: `groupadd deploy`, `groupdel contractors`, and `usermod -aG deploy alice`
options.why: `-aG` appends the named group to the account's existing supplementary list rather than replacing it.

options.text: The same two group commands, but dropping the `a` so it reads `usermod -G deploy alice`
options.why: Without `-a`, `-G` replaces the entire supplementary group list, which can silently drop every other group `alice` belonged to.

options.text: Reaching for the account-management pair `useradd deploy` and `userdel contractors` before the same `usermod -aG` step
options.why: Those commands create and remove user accounts rather than groups, so nothing about `deploy` or `contractors` as groups is actually built or removed.

options.text: Lower-casing the last step to `usermod -g deploy alice` while keeping the two group commands as written
options.why: Lowercase `-g` replaces the primary group entirely rather than adding a supplementary one, which is a different change than asked for.

items.rationale: `groupadd` and `groupdel` create and remove groups, and `usermod -aG` appends a supplementary group to an account without touching its existing memberships — the destructive alternative is `-G` alone, which replaces the whole list.

items.stem: Two accounts are created with different usernames but the administrator accidentally assigns them the same UID. What does the kernel treat them as, for permission purposes?

options.text: The same identity — the kernel enforces access by the numeric UID, not by the account name
options.why: Permission checks are made against the numeric UID the kernel holds, and both accounts share that number.

options.text: Two separate identities, because the account name is what the kernel checks
options.why: The name is a convenience for humans; the number is what the kernel actually enforces access against.

options.text: Two separate identities, because each has its own entry in `/etc/passwd`
options.why: A distinct row in the account database does not create a distinct identity if the numeric UID field is shared.

options.text: Two separate identities, distinguished by their primary group instead — the primary group affects new files created, not whose identity a process runs as
options.why: The primary group affects new files created, not whose identity a process runs as.

items.rationale: UID 0 is root regardless of what any account sharing it is called, and more generally the kernel checks the number rather than the name. Two accounts sharing a UID are indistinguishable to every permission check the kernel makes, even though `/etc/passwd` lists them as separate rows. `id` is the command that prints the UID and GID actually in force for a given account.

items.stem: A user belongs to `developers` as a supplementary group and `staff` as their primary group. Which group owns a file they create in their home directory with no special tooling involved?

options.text: `staff`, because a newly created file takes the creator's primary group
options.why: The primary group is exactly the one applied to a file at creation time, unless SGID or another mechanism overrides it.

options.text: `developers`, because supplementary groups grant access to newly created files too
options.why: Supplementary groups grant access to files that already exist; they do not become the owning group of a new one.

options.text: Whichever group appears first alphabetically among the ones the user belongs to
options.why: Group ownership follows the primary/supplementary distinction, not alphabetical order.

options.text: `root`, because only a privileged process can set group ownership on creation
options.why: An unprivileged process still creates files under its own primary group; no privilege is required for that.

items.rationale: Every user has exactly one primary group, and that is the group applied to files they create; supplementary groups only add access to files that already exist, unless a directory carries the SGID bit. `id` and `groups` both show the current membership; `usermod -g` changes the primary group, while `usermod -aG` appends a supplementary one.

items.stem: After running `usermod -G developers alice`, `alice` reports she can no longer access files under a project she previously worked on through another group. What happened?

options.text: `-G` without `-a` replaced her entire supplementary group list with just `developers`
options.why: Bare `-G` sets the complete supplementary list rather than adding to it, dropping every membership not named on the command line.

options.text: Her primary group was changed to `developers`, which does not affect existing file access
options.why: `-G` affects the supplementary list, not the primary group, and either way this would not explain losing access.

options.text: Nothing changed; supplementary group membership has no effect on file access
options.why: Supplementary groups are exactly what extend a user's access to files owned by a group other than their primary one.

options.text: The other project's group was deleted at the same time by an unrelated cleanup
options.why: Nothing in the scenario describes a group being deleted, and the command given fully explains the symptom on its own.

items.rationale: `usermod -G` without `-a` silently replaces the whole supplementary group list rather than adding to it — a classic destructive mistake. `usermod -aG developers alice` would have appended `developers` while leaving her other memberships intact.

items.stem: Counting the colon-separated fields of a line in `/etc/passwd` in order, which field is the login shell?

options.text: The seventh and last field
options.why: The order is username, password placeholder, UID, GID, comment, home directory, then login shell.

options.text: The sixth field, since the password placeholder is usually skipped when counting
options.why: The placeholder field is easy to forget, but it is still field two — omitting it miscounts everything after it by one.

options.text: The fourth field, the same position as the primary GID
options.why: The fourth field is the primary GID; the login shell comes three fields later.

options.text: It is not in `/etc/passwd` at all — login shells are recorded only in `/etc/shadow`
options.why: `/etc/shadow` holds password hashes and ageing data, not the login shell, which lives in `/etc/passwd`.

items.rationale: `/etc/passwd` has seven fields: username, password placeholder (x), UID, GID, comment/GECOS, home directory, and login shell. The placeholder is the field most often dropped when counting by memory, which shifts every later field. `getent passwd` is the NSS-aware way to look up a row without opening the file directly.

items.stem: An administrator runs `getent passwd alice` and sees `x` in the second field. What does that field actually hold today?

options.text: Nothing usable — it is a placeholder, and the real password hash lives in `/etc/shadow`
options.why: The name "password" field is historical; the hash moved to `/etc/shadow` and this field only marks that fact.

options.text: The account's password hash, still stored here as the field name suggests
options.why: Despite the field's name, the hash has not lived in `/etc/passwd` for decades — it is world-readable, which a hash cannot safely be.

options.text: The number of days until the password expires — expiry is tracked in `/etc/shadow`'s ageing fields, not in this world-readable file
options.why: Expiry is tracked in `/etc/shadow`'s ageing fields, not in this world-readable file.

options.text: The account's primary GID, encoded as the letter `x`
options.why: The GID is the next field over and is always numeric, not the placeholder character.

items.rationale: `/etc/passwd` is world-readable, so it cannot safely hold a password hash; the second field is a placeholder (`x` on most systems) pointing administrators at `/etc/shadow`, which is not world-readable and holds the real hash.

items.stem: A Debian-family server and a Red Hat-family server both protect `/etc/shadow` from ordinary users, but by different means. What are the two modes?

options.text: `0640 root:shadow` on Debian-family systems, and `0000 root:root` on Red Hat-family systems
options.why: Debian-family lets the `shadow` group read it under a non-zero mode; Red Hat-family ships no permission bits at all and relies on root bypassing checks.

options.text: `0644 root:root` on every distribution, since the file only needs to block writes
options.why: That mode would leave the file world-readable, exposing every password hash — exactly what shadowing exists to prevent.

options.text: `0600 root:root` universally, matching the private key convention
options.why: The two families do not converge on one mode; the permissions genuinely differ by family, which is the point being tested.

options.text: `0640 shadow:root` on both families, with the group and owner reversed from the Debian scheme
options.why: This reverses the actual Debian-family ownership, where `root` owns the file and `shadow` is the readable group.

items.rationale: Exact permissions are distribution-specific: Debian-family systems ship `/etc/shadow` as `0640 root:shadow` so the `shadow` group can read it, while Red Hat-family systems ship it `0000 root:root`, relying on root bypassing permission checks entirely. Neither figure should be stated as universal. `chage` is the tool for reading or changing the ageing fields this file holds.

items.stem: An administrator wants to force `bob` to pick a new password the next time he logs in, without disabling his account. Which change to `/etc/shadow` fields does that, and which command applies it?

options.text: Set the last-change field to `0` with `chage -d 0 bob`
options.why: A value of `0` in the last-change field means "must change at next login," which is exactly the stated goal.

options.text: Set the account expiry date with `chage -E`
options.why: An expiry date disables the account outright once reached, rather than merely prompting for a new password.

options.text: Edit `/etc/passwd` to clear the login shell field
options.why: The login shell controls what runs at login, not whether a password change is required — and it is the wrong file for ageing data.

options.text: Lock the account with `usermod -L`, which forces a password reset on next login
options.why: Locking prefixes the stored hash with `!` so no password matches at all — it prevents login rather than prompting for a new password.

items.rationale: `/etc/shadow` records the date of last password change as days since the epoch, and setting that field to `0` is the documented way to force a change at next login; `chage -d 0` sets it. Locking the account or setting an expiry date achieves a different outcome.

items.stem: How many colon-separated fields does a line in `/etc/group` have, and how does that compare with `/etc/passwd`?

options.text: Four fields in `/etc/group`, against seven in `/etc/passwd`
options.why: `/etc/group` records group name, password placeholder, GID, and the member list — fewer fields because a group carries less per-row data than an account.

options.text: Seven fields in both files, since they share the same layout convention
options.why: The two files describe different kinds of row and do not share a field count; `/etc/group` has fewer fields.

options.text: The reverse pairing — seven for `/etc/group` and four for `/etc/passwd`
options.why: This reverses the actual counts: `/etc/passwd` is the seven-field file describing an account.

options.text: Four fields in `/etc/group`, against nine in `/etc/passwd`
options.why: Nine is the field count for `/etc/shadow`, not `/etc/passwd`, which has seven.

items.rationale: `/etc/group` has four fields — group name, password placeholder, GID, and the comma-separated supplementary member list — against `/etc/passwd`'s seven, because one row describes an entire group rather than a single account's full set of attributes. `getent group` is the NSS-aware way to query a row rather than reading the file directly.

items.stem: `getent group developers` lists three members. A fourth user has `developers` as their primary group. Does that user appear in the output?

options.text: No — the member list in `/etc/group` records supplementary membership only
options.why: Primary membership is recorded on the user's own row in `/etc/passwd`, not in the group's member list.

options.text: Yes, every member of the group appears in the member list regardless of how they joined it
options.why: The field only ever lists supplementary members; anyone whose primary group this is will be missing from it.

options.text: No, because primary group membership is not recorded anywhere on the system
options.why: It is recorded — in field four of that user's `/etc/passwd` row — just not in `/etc/group`'s member list.

options.text: Yes, but only after running `groupadd` again to refresh the membership list
options.why: `groupadd` creates a group; it does not recompute or refresh any membership list.

items.rationale: The fourth field of `/etc/group` is the supplementary member list only. A user whose primary group is `developers` is recorded on their own `/etc/passwd` row, not in `/etc/group`, so answering "who is in this group" completely requires reading both files.

items.stem: An account must own a set of files and be usable as the identity a backup script runs under, but must never be usable to log in interactively. Which change accomplishes that?

options.text: Set its login shell to `/usr/sbin/nologin`
options.why: A nologin shell is exactly the standard mechanism for an account that must exist and own files but never provide an interactive session.

options.text: Lock the account's password with `passwd -l`
options.why: Locking blocks password authentication specifically, but key-based or other authentication methods can still start an interactive shell.

options.text: Delete the account's entry from `/etc/shadow`
options.why: Removing the shadow row breaks password authentication entirely and leaves the account in an inconsistent, unsupported state.

options.text: Set the account's UID to a value above 60000
options.why: A high UID is a convention for distinguishing service accounts visually; it has no effect on whether login is possible.

items.rationale: The login shell is the program started at login, and setting it to `/usr/sbin/nologin` is the standard way to create an account that owns files and can be used to run scheduled work but cannot be used to log in interactively. `chsh` is the ordinary command for changing which shell an account uses.

items.stem: An account's shell was changed to `/usr/sbin/nologin` last week, yet the account's existing SSH key still allows it to run one non-interactive command over SSH. Is that expected?

options.text: Yes — a nologin shell blocks an interactive session, but SSH can still run a single remote command through it
options.why: The restriction is specifically on starting an interactive shell; a non-interactive command execution is a different code path that nologin does not intercept in every configuration.

options.text: No, a nologin shell should have revoked every one of the account's SSH keys automatically
options.why: Changing the login shell does not touch authorised keys at all; the two are managed independently.

options.text: No, this indicates the password hash was never actually locked — whether the password is locked is unrelated to key-based SSH access, which does not use the password hash
options.why: Whether the password is locked is unrelated to key-based SSH access, which does not use the password hash.

options.text: Yes, because `nologin` only applies to accounts with a UID below 1000
options.why: The nologin shell has nothing to do with the UID range; it applies to whatever account it is set on.

items.rationale: A nologin shell is not a full account lock — it prevents an interactive shell from starting, but it does not by itself remove SSH authorised keys or other non-interactive access paths, which is why a service account with nologin can still be reachable for narrowly scoped remote commands.

items.stem: What is the purpose of creating a dedicated service account for a web server daemon rather than running it under an administrator's own account?

options.text: To limit the damage a compromised daemon can do, by giving it only the privilege it needs
options.why: A dedicated, unprivileged account bounds what an attacker gains if the daemon is compromised, which is the whole reason the practice exists.

options.text: To give the daemon a personal login so a human can use it to authenticate interactively
options.why: A service account exists to run a daemon, not to provide anyone with an interactive login.

options.text: To grant the daemon root access automatically, since service accounts are privileged by convention
options.why: A service account is created unprivileged by design; nothing about the category grants root automatically.

options.text: To let the daemon be scheduled with `cron` instead of `systemd`
options.why: Which scheduler runs a job is unrelated to whether it runs under a dedicated account.

items.rationale: A service account is an unprivileged account created to run a daemon rather than to be logged into, so that a compromised service is confined to whatever narrow privilege that account holds instead of an administrator's full access.

items.stem: An account has a system-range UID, a nologin shell, and no interactive password set, and it is the identity a database daemon runs under. Which term describes it, and is it automatically unprivileged?

options.text: A service account — and no, its actual privilege still depends entirely on what it was granted
options.why: "Service account" describes the account's purpose, not a guarantee about its power; it can still be over-granted like any other account.

options.text: A service account, and yes, service accounts are unprivileged by definition
options.why: Nothing about the category enforces low privilege automatically — a poorly configured service account can hold broad access just like any other account.

options.text: A regular user account, since it belongs to a specific named daemon
options.why: A regular user account is meant for a person to log into; this one is defined by running a daemon and having no interactive login.

options.text: A group, since it is shared by every process the daemon forks — the description is of a single account with a UID and a shell, not a group with a member list
options.why: The description is of a single account with a UID and a shell, not a group with a member list.

items.rationale: The description matches a service account: an unprivileged-by-intent identity for a daemon. But "unprivileged" is a design goal, not an automatic property — a service account can still be granted excessive privilege if it is configured that way.

items.stem: A policy requires every password to be changed at least every 90 days and to warn the user seven days beforehand. Which fields in `/etc/shadow`, changed through `chage`, enforce that?

options.text: The maximum age field (`-M 90`) and the warning period field (`-W 7`)
options.why: Maximum age bounds how long a password may stand before it must change, and the warning field controls how far ahead of that the user is notified.

options.text: The minimum age field (`-m 90`) and the account expiry field (`-E 7`)
options.why: Minimum age sets the earliest a password may be changed again, and expiry disables the account on a date — neither matches the stated 90-day/7-day requirement.

options.text: Password complexity settings, since ageing and complexity are the same policy category
options.why: Complexity rules govern what a password may contain; they say nothing about how often it must be changed, which is a separate policy.

options.text: The login shell field, set to a value that expires automatically after 90 days
options.why: The login shell has no expiry behaviour of any kind; it only names the program started at login.

items.rationale: `chage -M` sets the maximum password age and `chage -W` sets the warning period before expiry, both stored in `/etc/shadow`. Complexity requirements are a separate, unrelated policy category from ageing.

items.stem: A newly created account must be forced to set its own password the very first time it logs in, rather than continuing to use the temporary password an administrator assigned. Which command achieves that most directly?

options.text: `passwd -e alice`, which expires the current password immediately
options.why: Expiring the password forces a change at the very next authentication, which is exactly the stated requirement.

options.text: `chage -m 90 alice`, setting a 90-day minimum age
options.why: A minimum age controls how soon a password can be changed again; it does not force an immediate change.

options.text: `usermod -L alice`, locking the account
options.why: Locking prevents password authentication outright rather than prompting for a new password at next login.

options.text: `chsh alice`, changing the login shell — changing the shell affects what program starts at login, not whether the password must be renewed
options.why: Changing the shell affects what program starts at login, not whether the password must be renewed.

items.rationale: `passwd -e` expires an account's password immediately, which forces the user to set a new one at their next login — the direct way to retire a temporary administrator-assigned password.

items.stem: A directory is `d-wx------`. Its owner has write and execute but not read. Can the owner list the directory's contents with `ls`, and can they open a file inside it by name?

options.text: No to listing; yes to opening a known filename, because listing needs read while traversal needs execute
options.why: On a directory, read permission is what lets the contents be enumerated, and execute is what lets the directory be entered by name — the two are independent.

options.text: No to both, because any operation on a directory needs all three bits together
options.why: The three bits govern separate operations on a directory; execute alone is enough to traverse into it by a known name.

options.text: Yes to both, because write on a directory implies read for its owner — write on a directory means the owner may create or delete entries; it does not grant read, which is what listing requires
options.why: Write on a directory means the owner may create or delete entries; it does not grant read, which is what listing requires.

options.text: Yes to listing but no to opening a known file, since read must come before execute
options.why: This reverses the actual roles: read enables listing, execute enables traversal, and this directory has execute but not read.

items.rationale: On a directory, execute means "may traverse into" and is independent of read, which means "may list the entries." With `-wx` set and `r` absent, the owner can enter the directory and open a file whose name they already know, but cannot enumerate what is there with `ls`. `ls -l` and `chmod` are the ordinary tools for inspecting and changing that mode.

items.stem: After a bulk permission change, users report they can no longer traverse into a directory tree at all, though the files inside still show read permission when named directly by another process. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The directories in the tree lost their execute bit, blocking traversal even though file read bits are untouched
options.why: Traversal into a directory is governed by its own execute bit, independent of the read permission on the files it contains.

options.text: The files themselves must have lost their write permission — write permission on the files controls whether their contents can be changed, not whether the directory holding them can be entered
options.why: Write permission on the files controls whether their contents can be changed, not whether the directory holding them can be entered.

options.text: The owning group of the directories was changed to one nobody belongs to
options.why: A group change would affect the group triad's access, but the scenario describes a traversal failure consistent with a missing execute bit specifically.

options.text: The umask was changed on the server, retroactively affecting the existing tree
options.why: A umask only affects the permissions given to newly created files and directories; it cannot retroactively change an existing tree.

items.rationale: Traversal requires execute on every directory along the path, independent of what the files inside allow. A bulk change that strips execute from directories — a common side effect of an overly broad `chmod -R` — produces exactly this symptom.

items.stem: A file is `-rw-r-----`, owned by `alice` and belonging to group `staff`, of which `alice` is also a member. Can `alice` write to it?

options.text: Yes, because the kernel matches the owner class first and grants read and write there
options.why: The owner triad is checked first and, once matched, the group and other triads are never consulted for that user.

options.text: No, because being a member of the owning group means the more restrictive group bits apply
options.why: Class matching stops at the first match; membership in the group does not pull a more restrictive triad in for the owner.

options.text: Only if the `other` triad also grants write, since all three classes must agree
options.why: Classes do not need to agree with one another; only the first matching class is consulted at all.

options.text: No, because `alice` would need to be listed in `/etc/group` to use owner privileges
options.why: Owner privilege comes from being the file's owner, not from appearing in the group's supplementary member list.

items.rationale: The kernel checks owner, group, and other in that order and stops at the first class that applies. `alice` is the owner, so the owner triad (`rw-`) governs her access regardless of what the group or other triads say, as read directly from `ls -l`.

items.stem: A file is `-r--rw-rw-`. Its owner removes all permission from the `other` class, leaving `-r--rw----`. Does that change what the owner can do to the file?

options.text: No — removing permission from `other` never restricts the owner or group classes
options.why: Each class is evaluated independently once matched; narrowing `other` has no bearing on what the owner's own triad allows.

options.text: Yes, narrowing any one class tightens the effective permission for everyone
options.why: Permission classes do not combine or narrow one another; each is a self-contained answer for the users it applies to.

options.text: Yes, because the owner's access is always the most restrictive of the three classes
options.why: The owner's access is whatever the owner triad states, not a function of the other two classes.

options.text: It depends on whether the sticky bit is also set on the file
options.why: The sticky bit governs deletion within a directory and has no bearing on a regular file's own read/write bits.

items.rationale: The owner is still matched by the owner triad, which was untouched by narrowing `other`. Removing access from one class narrows only that class's users; it does not tighten or loosen either of the other two.

items.stem: A file is `rwxr-xr-x` with the setgid bit already set for a shared workflow. An administrator must add write for the group without disturbing anything else, including the setgid bit. Which command is safe?

options.text: `chmod g+w file`, a symbolic clause that changes only the named bit
options.why: Symbolic mode changes are relative: `g+w` adds group write and leaves every other bit, including setgid, exactly as it was.

options.text: `chmod 775 file`, since 775 already includes group write
options.why: A three-digit numeric mode is absolute and rewrites all nine permission bits plus clears the special-bit digit, silently dropping the setgid bit.

options.text: `umask 002` applied before the next write to the file — a umask only affects permissions assigned to files created afterward; it has no effect on a file that already exists
options.why: A umask only affects permissions assigned to files created afterward; it has no effect on a file that already exists.

options.text: `chmod -R g+w file`, adding the recursive flag for safety
options.why: Recursion is unnecessary and potentially harmful on a single file; the target here is one file, not a tree.

items.rationale: Symbolic mode expresses a relative change: `g+w` adds exactly the group-write bit and leaves the rest, including the setgid special bit, untouched. A three-digit numeric mode like `775` is absolute and always clears the setuid/setgid/sticky digit unless it is explicitly included — both are forms of the same `chmod` command, and the notation chosen changes what survives.

items.stem: After running `chmod 755` across a directory tree that previously had setgid directories for a shared team folder, the team reports new files are no longer inheriting the shared group. What happened, and how should it be fixed?

options.text: The three-digit numeric mode cleared the setgid bit on every directory; the fix is `chmod 2755` or the symbolic form `g+s`
options.why: A three-digit mode is absolute and always clears the leading special-bit digit unless a fourth digit restores it, which is exactly the observed symptom.

options.text: Nothing was cleared; `chmod 755` is equivalent to the earlier setgid mode — `755` omits the leading digit entirely, and an omitted digit is treated as zero, so any special bit that was set is gone
options.why: `755` omits the leading digit entirely, and an omitted digit is treated as zero, so any special bit that was set is gone.

options.text: The group ownership of the directories reverted to root, unrelated to any permission bit
options.why: The symptom described — new files not inheriting the group — is the signature of a lost setgid bit, not a change of directory ownership.

options.text: The umask on the team's shell sessions must have changed at the same time
options.why: A umask affects the base permissions of new files, not whether they inherit the directory's group, which is what setgid controls.

items.rationale: A three-digit octal mode is absolute: omitted digits are treated as leading zeros, so `chmod 755` clears any setuid, setgid, or sticky bit that was previously set. Restoring the behaviour needs either a four-digit numeric mode (`2755`) or the symbolic form (`chmod g+s`), which changes only the named bit.

items.stem: A file was copied as root into `alice`'s home directory and is now owned by root. `alice` wants to take ownership herself. Can she run `chown alice file` to do it?

options.text: No — only a privileged process may give a file away to another user; `alice` cannot chown it to herself either
options.why: Changing the owning user is restricted to a process with the capability root normally holds, regardless of who the target owner is.

options.text: Yes, any user may change the ownership of a file they can currently read
options.why: Read access has no bearing on the ownership-change privilege, which is restricted regardless of what the caller can already do with the file.

options.text: Yes, but only because she is changing it to her own account rather than someone else's
options.why: The restriction applies to the operation itself, not to whether the target happens to be the caller — an ordinary user cannot chown a file at all.

options.text: No, but `chgrp` would work instead since group changes are unrestricted — it is not unrestricted, and it does not change the owner
options.why: An unprivileged user may change a file's group, but only to a group they belong to — it is not unrestricted, and it does not change the owner.

items.rationale: Only a privileged process may change a file's owning user, so `alice` must ask an administrator to run `chown alice file` as root. An unprivileged user may change the group of a file they own, but only to a group they themselves belong to, which is a narrower privilege.

items.stem: What is the difference between `chown alice file` and `chown alice: file`?

options.text: The bare form changes only the owning user; the trailing colon also sets the group to `alice`'s login group
options.why: A trailing colon with nothing after it tells `chown` to set the group to the named user's own login group as well.

options.text: There is no difference — the trailing colon is a harmless stylistic choice — the colon is meaningful syntax: its presence, even with nothing following it, adds a group change to the command
options.why: The colon is meaningful syntax: its presence, even with nothing following it, adds a group change to the command.

options.text: `chown alice: file` changes the group only, leaving the owning user untouched
options.why: The bare user name before the colon still sets the owner; the colon adds a group change on top of it rather than replacing it.

options.text: `chown alice: file` requires `alice` to already own the file, unlike the bare form
options.why: Both forms are subject to the same ownership-change restriction; the colon does not add or remove that requirement.

items.rationale: `chown alice file` changes only the owning user. `chown alice: file` — with a trailing colon and nothing after it — additionally sets the group to `alice`'s own login group, which is a separate and easily missed effect of the syntax.

items.stem: With `umask 022` in effect, what mode does a newly created regular file receive, given that programs typically request `0666` for a new file?

options.text: `644`, because the umask subtracts write for group and other from the requested `666`
options.why: A umask of `022` removes write from the group and other classes, turning the requested `666` into `644`.

options.text: `022`, because the umask is applied directly as the resulting mode
options.why: A umask is a mask of bits to remove, not the mode itself — it never becomes the file's permissions verbatim.

options.text: `755`, the same result `chmod 755` would produce on the file — the two are not interchangeable
options.why: A umask acts on future file creation and subtracts bits; `chmod 755` is an absolute, present-tense change to an existing file — the two are not interchangeable.

options.text: `666`, since a umask only affects directories, not regular files
options.why: A umask affects both files and directories created afterward; regular files are not exempt from it.

items.rationale: A umask subtracts bits from the mode a program requests when creating a file. Programs conventionally request `0666` for a regular file, and a umask of `022` removes write from group and other, leaving `644`. The umask cannot grant permission — only remove it. The `umask` command reports or sets the current mask for a shell session.

items.stem: Why can an ordinary, unprivileged user successfully run `passwd` to change their own password, when `passwd` needs to write to `/etc/shadow`, which the user cannot open directly?

options.text: `passwd` carries the set-user-ID bit, so it runs with the file owner's (root's) privileges rather than the caller's
options.why: SUID makes the running process take on the effective UID of the file's owner, which is exactly the controlled privilege escalation this scenario needs.

options.text: The user's real UID temporarily becomes root's for the duration of the command — sUID changes the effective UID, not the real UID; the real UID still records who actually launched the process
options.why: SUID changes the effective UID, not the real UID; the real UID still records who actually launched the process.

options.text: `passwd` carries the set-group-ID bit, running with the group `shadow`'s privileges
options.why: On Debian-family systems a shadow-group helper is one real design, but the textbook answer for `passwd` itself is the set-user-ID bit running as root.

options.text: The user is temporarily added to the `sudoers` file for the duration of the command
options.why: `passwd` does not consult or modify `sudoers`; its escalation comes entirely from the SUID bit on the binary itself.

items.rationale: The set-user-ID bit makes an executable run with the file owner's effective UID rather than the caller's. `passwd` is owned by root and carries this bit, which is how an ordinary user's invocation of it can write into `/etc/shadow`, a file they cannot otherwise open. Every SUID binary on a system can be enumerated with `find / -perm -4000`.

items.stem: An administrator runs `chmod u+s deploy.sh` on a shell script, expecting it to run with the file owner's privileges the way a compiled SUID binary would. It does not. Why?

options.text: Linux ignores the set-user-ID bit on interpreted scripts, so the bit is set but never takes effect
options.why: The kernel refuses to grant privilege to an interpreter reading a script it has not verified, so a script's SUID bit is inert by design.

options.text: The bit was not actually set, since `chmod u+s` silently fails on non-executable files
options.why: The script is executable, and `chmod u+s` succeeds on it; the bit is present, it simply has no effect for the kernel to honour on a script.

options.text: The script needs the sticky bit as well before setuid takes effect
options.why: The sticky bit governs deletion within a directory and has no bearing on whether setuid applies to an executable script.

options.text: The script must first be made SGID before SUID has any effect — sUID and SGID are independent bits; neither is a prerequisite for the other to take effect on an executable
options.why: SUID and SGID are independent bits; neither is a prerequisite for the other to take effect on an executable.

items.rationale: Linux deliberately ignores the set-user-ID bit on scripts: the kernel will not grant privilege to an interpreter that has not itself been verified to run safely with elevated rights. The bit can be set with `chmod u+s` and will show as `s` in `ls -l`, but it does nothing for an interpreted file.

items.stem: A team wants a shared directory where every file a member creates is automatically writable by the whole team, without each person having to `chgrp` and `chmod` after every save. Which combination builds that?

options.text: `chgrp developers /srv/shared`, `chmod 2770 /srv/shared`, and a umask of `002` in members' sessions
options.why: Setgid makes new files inherit the directory's group, and a `002` umask leaves group write intact on those new files — together they give exactly the described behaviour.

options.text: `chmod 4770 /srv/shared` alone, since setuid on a directory gives every file the owner's privileges
options.why: Set-user-ID has no defined meaning on a directory in Linux; only setgid and the sticky bit have directory semantics.

options.text: `chmod u+s /srv/shared`, since it runs new files with the file owner's privileges
options.why: That is the setuid bit, which has no effect on a directory; the group-inheritance behaviour needed here comes from setgid.

options.text: Adding the sticky bit to `/srv/shared` so files inherit the shared group
options.why: The sticky bit restricts who may delete an entry; it has no effect on which group new files inherit.

items.rationale: Setgid on a directory, set with `chmod g+s` or the numeric `2770`, makes newly created entries inherit the directory's group rather than the creator's primary group. That alone still leaves new files with whatever the umask allows, so a `002` umask is needed too, or teammates still cannot write to each other's files.

items.stem: A directory already has `chmod 2770 /srv/shared` applied for a shared team folder. Files that already existed before that change still cannot be edited by other members. What is going on?

options.text: Setgid inheritance applies only to entries created after the bit was set, not retroactively to existing files
options.why: The bit changes what happens at creation time; it has no effect on files that were already present in the directory.

options.text: The setgid bit was not actually applied, since `2770` should have fixed every file in the directory
options.why: The mode was applied successfully to the directory; the symptom is expected, because setgid never rewrites existing entries.

options.text: The files need the sticky bit removed before they can be shared — the sticky bit restricts deletion, not editing, and has nothing to do with whether teammates can write to a file
options.why: The sticky bit restricts deletion, not editing, and has nothing to do with whether teammates can write to a file.

options.text: The files must individually be given the setuid bit to be shared
options.why: Setuid on a regular file changes which identity it runs as if executed; it has no bearing on ordinary read/write sharing of data files.

items.rationale: Setgid on a directory affects only entries created after the bit is set; existing files keep whatever group and mode they already had. The fix for pre-existing files is a one-time `chgrp` and `chmod` pass, after which the setgid bit keeps everything new consistent going forward.

items.stem: `/tmp` is world-writable, `drwxrwxrwt`. Name every party who may still delete or rename a file inside it that they do not own.

options.text: The file's owner, the directory's owner, and a privileged process — nobody else
options.why: The sticky bit narrows directory write from "may remove any entry" to exactly these three parties, which is the whole reason `/tmp` can be world-writable safely.

options.text: Only the file's owner — write permission on the directory does not matter once the sticky bit is set
options.why: This is the recurring error: the directory's owner and a privileged process may also remove an entry, not the file's owner alone.

options.text: Any user with write permission on the directory, since the sticky bit only affects renaming, not deletion
options.why: The sticky bit restricts both renaming and deletion equally; it does not carve out deletion as unaffected.

options.text: Only a privileged process, since `/tmp` is meant to be fully protected from ordinary users
options.why: Ordinary users routinely delete their own files in `/tmp`; the restriction is narrower than blocking every ordinary user.

items.rationale: The sticky bit, set with `chmod +t`, restricts deletion and renaming inside a shared-writable directory to three parties: the file's own owner, the directory's owner, and a privileged process. Naming only "the file's owner" and forgetting the other two is the standard way this fact is gotten wrong.

items.stem: `ls -ld /srv/scratch` shows `drwxrwxr-T`. What does the capital `T` indicate, compared to a lowercase `t`?

options.text: The sticky bit is set, but other-execute is not, so the directory is untraversable by anyone outside owner and group
options.why: A capital letter in that position always signals a bit set alongside a missing execute bit for that class, which here makes the directory unreachable to `other`.

options.text: The capital letter means the sticky bit is somehow "stronger" than lowercase
options.why: Case does not indicate strength; it indicates whether the corresponding execute bit is also present, which changes traversal rather than the protection itself.

options.text: It means the setgid bit is active in addition to the sticky bit
options.why: Setgid would appear as `s` or `S` in the group triad, a different position from the sticky bit shown here in the other triad.

options.text: It is a typo in the output and should be read as lowercase `t` — the distinction between the two cases is meaningful output, not an error, and changes what the mode string is telling you
options.why: The distinction between the two cases is meaningful output, not an error, and changes what the mode string is telling you.

items.rationale: In the other triad's execute position, lowercase `t` means the sticky bit is set and execute is also present; uppercase `T` means the sticky bit is set but execute is not, which — on a directory — makes it untraversable to anyone outside the owner and group, usually unintentionally.

items.stem: An administrator argues that logging in via `sudo -i` and staying in that root shell all afternoon satisfies least privilege, because `sudo` was used rather than `su`. Is that correct?

options.text: No — an all-afternoon root shell holds the same authority either way; least privilege is about how much and how long, not which command opened it
options.why: The principle concerns the scope and duration of the privilege actually held, and an extended root shell is the same exposure regardless of the command that started it.

options.text: Yes, because `sudo` always logs individual commands, which by itself satisfies least privilege
options.why: `sudo -i` opens a shell, and commands run inside it are not individually logged the way single-command invocations are — logging is not what the principle is measuring here in any case.

options.text: Yes, because `sudo` requires the administrator's own password rather than the root password
options.why: Which password authenticates the session is a separate question from how much privilege is then held and for how long.

options.text: No, but only because `sudo -i` is slower to authenticate with than `su -` — authentication speed has nothing to do with the least-privilege principle; the issue is the breadth and duration of access held
options.why: Authentication speed has nothing to do with the least-privilege principle; the issue is the breadth and duration of access held.

items.rationale: Least privilege is about granting the smallest privilege sufficient for the task, for the shortest time. An all-afternoon `sudo -i` session holds full root authority for as long as `su -` would, so the choice of command does not by itself satisfy the principle.

items.stem: A file is `chmod 000`, owned by root. Can a process running as root read and write it despite the mode granting no bits to anyone?

options.text: Yes — root bypasses the ordinary permission check entirely, so the mode bits are irrelevant to it
options.why: Being UID 0 means the kernel skips the permission comparison altogether for that process, regardless of what the mode string says.

options.text: No, `000` blocks every process including root, since the mode has no bits set for any class
options.why: Root is not subject to the same check the mode bits express; it is exactly why Red Hat-family systems can ship `/etc/shadow` at `0000` and still have it work.

options.text: Only if root is also the file's owner, which grants an exception to the check
options.why: Root's bypass does not depend on ownership of the specific file; it applies to root's access generally.

options.text: Only through `sudo`, since plain root access still respects file modes — a process running as root, whether reached via `sudo`, `su`, or direct login, is subject to the same kernel-level bypass
options.why: A process running as root, whether reached via `sudo`, `su`, or direct login, is subject to the same kernel-level bypass.

items.rationale: Root is UID 0, the identity for which the kernel's ordinary permission checks are bypassed entirely. A mode of `000` blocks every other identity, but a root process is unaffected by mode bits at all — which is exactly why some distributions can ship sensitive files with no permission bits set.

items.stem: An organisation wants a per-command audit trail of every administrative action, showing exactly who ran what. Should administrators be told to use `sudo` for individual commands, or `su -` for a shell?

options.text: `sudo` for individual commands — it logs each invocation, while `su -` only logs the single switch to a shell
options.why: Once inside an `su -` shell everything run is anonymous within that shell, whereas `sudo` records each command as it is run.

options.text: `su -`, since it requires the target account's own password and is therefore more accountable
options.why: Requiring the target's password authenticates the switch; it does not create a record of what is done afterward inside that shell.

options.text: Either is equivalent for auditing, since both ultimately grant root access — `sudo` scoped to commands is specifically what preserves per-action logging
options.why: Holding the same privilege level does not mean the same audit trail — `sudo` scoped to commands is specifically what preserves per-action logging.

options.text: `sudo -i`, since it combines the audit benefit of `sudo` with a full login shell
options.why: `sudo -i` opens a shell just as `su -` does; commands run inside it are not individually logged the way single-command `sudo` invocations are.

items.rationale: `sudo` run per command logs what was executed and by whom, because each invocation is authenticated and recorded separately. `su -` authenticates once and hands over an entire shell, after which everything typed is anonymous within that session as far as the audit trail is concerned.

items.stem: On a fresh Ubuntu installation, an administrator runs `su` to become root and it fails no matter what password is entered, even though `sudo` works fine for the same account. Why?

options.text: Root's password is locked by default on Ubuntu, so `su` to root always fails; `sudo -i` is the intended route to a root shell instead
options.why: A locked root password makes `su` unusable regardless of what is typed, and Ubuntu deliberately routes administration through `sudo` instead.

options.text: The administrator has forgotten the root password and must reset it before `su` will work
options.why: The account is not merely forgotten — it is locked by the distribution's design, so no password will ever satisfy it until it is explicitly unlocked.

options.text: `su` requires the caller to already be a member of the `sudo` group — `su` authenticates against the target account's own password; group membership in `sudo` is what governs whether `sudo` itself is permitted
options.why: `su` authenticates against the target account's own password; group membership in `sudo` is what governs whether `sudo` itself is permitted.

options.text: `su` is disabled entirely on Ubuntu and cannot be used under any circumstances
options.why: The command is present and works to switch into any account whose password is set; only the root account specifically is locked by default.

items.rationale: On Ubuntu, and on any Debian installation where no root password was set during setup, the root account's password is locked, so `su` to root fails regardless of what is typed. The intended route to a root shell is `sudo -i`, which authenticates with the caller's own password instead.

items.stem: Why does `visudo` exist instead of editing `/etc/sudoers` with a normal text editor?

options.text: It validates the syntax before installing the file, so a mistake cannot lock every administrator out of privilege escalation at once
options.why: Because a broken sudoers file makes `sudo` refuse the whole policy, `visudo` checks the result before it ever takes effect.

options.text: It is only a convenience wrapper that opens the file in a nicer editor with syntax highlighting
options.why: The validation step is the substantive purpose; a plain editor with highlighting would still allow an unparseable file to be saved and installed.

options.text: It encrypts the sudoers file so its contents cannot be read by anyone but root — sudoers is a plain-text policy file; `visudo`'s role is validating syntax, not encrypting the file's contents
options.why: Sudoers is a plain-text policy file; `visudo`'s role is validating syntax, not encrypting the file's contents.

options.text: It is required because `/etc/sudoers` cannot otherwise be opened by any editor
options.why: The file can be opened by any editor; nothing technically prevents that. The reason to avoid it is the lack of a safety check before saving.

items.rationale: `visudo` locks the file against simultaneous edits, runs an editor, then parses the result and refuses to install it if there is a syntax error — printing the offending line and offering to re-edit. A plain editor has no such check, and a broken sudoers file makes `sudo` refuse its entire policy for everyone.

items.stem: `sudo` has stopped working for every user on a server after a configuration change earlier today. What is the diagnostic order for recovering, starting from a surviving root session?

options.text: Run `visudo -c` to see whether the main file parses, then check every drop-in under `/etc/sudoers.d/`, since a broken drop-in produces the same symptom
options.why: A parse failure anywhere in the policy — the main file or an included drop-in — makes `sudo` refuse everything, so checking syntax first isolates the fault fastest.

options.text: Delete `/etc/sudoers` and let the package manager regenerate a default copy — deleting the policy file removes the ability to reason about what changed and is far more destructive than checking syntax with `visudo -c` first
options.why: Deleting the policy file removes the ability to reason about what changed and is far more destructive than checking syntax with `visudo -c` first.

options.text: Reboot the server, since a sudoers problem is always resolved by a fresh boot
options.why: Rebooting does not repair a syntax error in a text file; the broken policy would still be in force after restart.

options.text: Run `chmod 777 /etc/sudoers` so every user can bypass the broken policy temporarily
options.why: Opening the file to everyone is both unsafe and beside the point — `sudo` refuses a policy that fails to parse regardless of who can read it.

items.rationale: A file that fails to parse is not partially applied — `sudo` refuses the whole policy, not just the broken line. From a surviving root session, `visudo -c` checks the main file, and because `visudo -c` also validates included files, checking `/etc/sudoers.d/` next catches a broken drop-in with the same symptom.

items.stem: Two people log in separately and each run the same text editor program. How many processes exist, and what identifies each one uniquely?

options.text: Two processes, each with its own PID — one program on disk can be running as many separate processes at once
options.why: A process is a running instance, not the file on disk, so each independent invocation gets its own PID even though the underlying program is identical.

options.text: One process, since only one copy of the program exists on disk
options.why: The file on disk is the program; each execution of it is a separate process with its own memory and PID, regardless of how many copies of the file exist.

options.text: Two services, one per user session — neither invocation is managed by an init system with a restart policy, so "service" is not the right term for either
options.why: Neither invocation is managed by an init system with a restart policy, so "service" is not the right term for either.

options.text: One process with two PPIDs, one for each user
options.why: A process has exactly one parent and therefore one PPID; two independent invocations are two separate processes, not one with two parents.

items.rationale: A process is a running instance of a program: its own PID, address space, open files, and credentials. One program file can be executed many times over, producing as many independent processes, each separately identified by its PID.

items.stem: A process appears idle in a snapshot from `ps` but `top` shows it pegged at 100% CPU. Which reading is correct?

options.text: Both can be correct at once — `ps` reports a total divided over the process's whole lifetime, while `top` samples over a short recent interval
options.why: The two commands answer different questions: a lifetime average can look low even while the current sampled rate is high, especially for a process with short, intense bursts.

options.text: One of the two tools must be malfunctioning, since they disagree about the same process
options.why: Disagreement is expected and does not indicate a fault — the tools compute genuinely different statistics rather than reporting the same one two ways.

options.text: `top`'s figure is always more accurate because it updates continuously
options.why: Neither figure is more "accurate" than the other; they measure different things, and continuous updating does not make one the correct answer to the other's question.

options.text: The process must have forked a hidden child that `ps` is not counting — nothing in the scenario suggests a fork; the discrepancy is fully explained by the different measurement windows the two tools use
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests a fork; the discrepancy is fully explained by the different measurement windows the two tools use.

items.rationale: `ps` reports CPU time as a share of the process's entire lifetime, while `top` reports CPU share over the interval since its last screen refresh. A process bursting briefly can look idle to the lifetime average and busy to the recent sample without either tool being wrong.

items.stem: What is PID 1, and what happens to a process whose parent has exited before it does?

options.text: PID 1 is the init system, the ancestor of every other process, and an orphaned process is re-parented to it
options.why: The kernel starts PID 1 first and reassigns any orphan to it, which is why PID 1 always shows up as the ultimate ancestor in a process tree.

options.text: PID 1 is reserved for the kernel itself, and an orphaned process is simply terminated
options.why: PID 1 is a user-space init process, not the kernel, and an orphan is re-parented rather than killed outright.

options.text: PID 1 is whichever process currently has the highest CPU priority — pID number assignment has nothing to do with scheduling priority; PID 1 is fixed as the first process the kernel starts
options.why: PID number assignment has nothing to do with scheduling priority; PID 1 is fixed as the first process the kernel starts.

options.text: An orphaned process becomes a zombie until an administrator manually reaps it
options.why: Orphaning and becoming a zombie are different outcomes — an orphan is re-parented and continues running; a zombie has already exited.

items.rationale: The kernel starts PID 1 first — the init system — and it becomes the ancestor of everything else. When a process's parent dies before it does, the kernel re-parents it to PID 1 rather than terminating it. `ps -ef` prints PID and PPID side by side, and `pgrep` finds PIDs by name or attribute.

items.stem: A stale monitoring script keeps a PID recorded in a file from an hour ago and sends it a signal to check on a long-running job. The signal reaches an entirely unrelated process instead. What explains this?

options.text: PIDs are reused once a process exits, so the recorded number may now belong to a different process entirely
options.why: The kernel reallocates exited processes' PIDs, so a stale record can silently point at a completely different, unrelated process later.

options.text: PID files are guaranteed unique for the life of the machine and cannot be reused
options.why: PIDs wrap and are reused once `pid_max` is reached, and more simply, as soon as the original process exits its number becomes available again.

options.text: The script must be running inside a different PID namespace than the job it is checking
options.why: Namespace differences change what number a process sees for itself, but nothing in this scenario describes containers or namespaces.

options.text: The job's PPID must have changed, which the script failed to account for — a changed PPID would affect parentage lookups, not which process a plain PID-based signal is delivered to
options.why: A changed PPID would affect parentage lookups, not which process a plain PID-based signal is delivered to.

items.rationale: PIDs identify a process only while it lives; once it exits, the kernel is free to reuse that number for something else. A PID recorded in a file and used later without checking is a well-known source of signalling the wrong process, which is why service managers prefer tracking by cgroup instead.

items.stem: A long-running job is started interactively in the foreground of an SSH session and then suspended with Ctrl-Z. Which two commands move it to the background and later bring it back?

options.text: `bg` to resume it in the background, and `fg` to bring it back to the foreground later
options.why: `bg` sends SIGCONT and lets the stopped job continue running in the background; `fg` reattaches the terminal to it afterward.

options.text: `nohup` to resume it in the background, since it is designed to keep a job running
options.why: `nohup` only makes a process immune to the hangup signal; it does not resume a job that Ctrl-Z has stopped, and it does not background anything by itself.

options.text: `jobs` to resume it in the background, and `kill` to bring it back — `jobs` only lists the current jobs; it does not change any job's state, and `kill` sends a signal rather than restoring foreground attachment
options.why: `jobs` only lists the current jobs; it does not change any job's state, and `kill` sends a signal rather than restoring foreground attachment.

options.text: Pressing Ctrl-C to resume it, then Ctrl-Z again to bring it forward
options.why: Ctrl-C sends SIGINT, which typically terminates the job rather than resuming a stopped one; Ctrl-Z only ever suspends.

items.rationale: Ctrl-Z suspends the foreground job with SIGTSTP. `bg` sends SIGCONT and lets it continue running in the background under a job number such as `%1`; `fg` later brings that same job back to the foreground and reattaches the terminal.

items.stem: A job was started with `./long-job.sh &` over SSH and the connection later drops. The job dies along with it, even though `&` was used. What was missing?

options.text: `nohup`, so the job is immune to the SIGHUP sent when the terminal closes
options.why: When a terminal closes, the kernel sends SIGHUP to its foreground process group and most shells forward it to background jobs too, which is what `&` alone does not prevent.

options.text: Nothing was missing; `&` alone is sufficient to survive a dropped connection
options.why: Backgrounding with `&` returns the prompt but leaves the job still attached to the shell, which is exactly what a hangup signal on disconnect can kill.

options.text: The job should have been started with `renice` instead of `&`
options.why: `renice` adjusts scheduling priority for an already-running process; it has no bearing on whether a job survives a terminal hangup.

options.text: The job needed to be run as a daemon rather than backgrounded with a shell operator
options.why: Converting it into a properly detached daemon would also work, but the direct and much simpler fix for this scenario is `nohup`.

items.rationale: `&` returns the prompt but the job is still the terminal session's child, so the SIGHUP sent on hangup is usually forwarded to it and kills it. `nohup` makes the command immune to that specific signal, which is the missing half of surviving a dropped SSH session.

items.stem: A daemon needs to shut down and should be given the chance to flush buffers, close files, and release its lock before it stops. Which signal, and which command, is the right first move?

options.text: SIGTERM, sent with plain `kill <pid>`, since it asks the process to shut down and can be caught
options.why: `kill` sends SIGTERM by default, and unlike SIGKILL it can be caught by a handler that performs an orderly shutdown.

options.text: SIGKILL, sent with `kill -9 <pid>`, to guarantee the process actually stops
options.why: SIGKILL removes the process from the scheduler immediately with no chance to clean up, which is the opposite of what an orderly shutdown needs as a first move.

options.text: SIGSTOP, to pause the process before deciding what to do next — sIGSTOP freezes the process rather than asking it to exit, and it cannot be caught or handled by the program at all
options.why: SIGSTOP freezes the process rather than asking it to exit, and it cannot be caught or handled by the program at all.

options.text: SIGHUP, since it is the standard signal for terminating a daemon cleanly
options.why: SIGHUP is conventionally used to ask a daemon to reload its configuration, not to terminate it.

items.rationale: `kill` sends SIGTERM by default, which a well-behaved daemon can catch to flush buffers, close files, and release locks before exiting. SIGKILL should be reserved for a process that does not respond, since it gives no opportunity to clean up. `killall` and `pkill` send the same signals but select processes by name or pattern rather than by PID.

items.stem: `kill -9` is sent to a process stuck reading from an unresponsive network filesystem, and the process is still there afterward. What explains this apparent failure?

options.text: The process is in uninterruptible sleep, waiting inside the kernel on I/O, and cannot be reaped until that I/O returns or times out
options.why: A process blocked in the kernel on I/O is not in a position to respond to any signal, including SIGKILL, until the kernel call it is stuck in resolves.

options.text: SIGKILL failed and a stronger signal such as `-15` should be tried instead — sIGTERM (signal 15) is weaker than SIGKILL, not stronger, and neither signal can reach a process stuck in uninterruptible sleep
options.why: SIGTERM (signal 15) is weaker than SIGKILL, not stronger, and neither signal can reach a process stuck in uninterruptible sleep.

options.text: The process must actually be a zombie, which explains why it cannot be killed
options.why: A zombie has already exited and holds only a table entry; this process is still actively blocked on I/O, a different state entirely.

options.text: `kill -9` only works on processes owned by the caller, and this one must belong to another user
options.why: Ownership would produce a permission error immediately, not a process that appears to survive the signal indefinitely.

items.rationale: A process in uninterruptible sleep (state `D` in `ps`) is blocked inside a kernel call waiting on I/O and cannot respond to any signal, SIGKILL included, until that call returns. This, along with an already-dead zombie, is the standard explanation for an apparent "kill -9 did nothing" report.

items.stem: An unprivileged user wants to lower the nice value of their own running batch job from 10 to 0, to give it more CPU time. Can they do it with plain `renice`?

options.text: No — lowering a nice value requires root or `CAP_SYS_NICE`, unless the administrator has raised `RLIMIT_NICE`, which by default allows no reduction
options.why: Raising your own niceness is always permitted, but lowering it back down needs privilege that an ordinary user does not hold unless a resource limit has been explicitly relaxed.

options.text: Yes, any user may freely move their own process's nice value in either direction
options.why: Movement is asymmetric: raising is unrestricted, but lowering — even back toward a value the user held before — needs privilege by default.

options.text: Yes, but only using `nice` rather than `renice`, since they behave differently for this purpose
options.why: Both commands are subject to the same privilege rule for lowering a nice value; the restriction is not specific to one command over the other.

options.text: No, because only the process's original parent may ever change its nice value — the restriction is about privilege level, not about parentage; a sufficiently privileged unrelated user or process can lower it too
options.why: The restriction is about privilege level, not about parentage; a sufficiently privileged unrelated user or process can lower it too.

items.rationale: Raising a process's own nice value — making it less demanding — is always allowed. Lowering it back down requires root or `CAP_SYS_NICE`, unless the administrator has raised the process's `RLIMIT_NICE` resource limit, which by default allows no reduction at all.

items.stem: A batch job is niced all the way down to 19 but a database it is supposedly starving is still slow. `top` shows the machine is not CPU-bound; memory usage is very high and swap activity is heavy. Will renicing the batch job further help?

options.text: No — nice only biases CPU scheduling, and it does nothing for memory pressure or I/O waits
options.why: Nice is a bias on who wins CPU time when the CPU is contended; on a machine limited by memory rather than CPU, adjusting it changes nothing.

options.text: Yes, renicing always frees resources across the board for the higher-priority process
options.why: A nice value affects scheduling priority only; it has no mechanism for reclaiming memory or reducing I/O wait for any other process.

options.text: Yes, but only if the batch job is also sent SIGSTOP first
options.why: Stopping the job would free some memory temporarily, but that is a different action from renicing and not what the question is asking about.

options.text: No, because nice values only take effect immediately after a process starts, not while it runs
options.why: `renice` is specifically designed to change the nice value of an already-running process, so timing after start is not the issue here.

items.rationale: Nice is a scheduling bias, not a reservation, and it affects only how CPU time is allocated when the CPU is contended. A machine that is memory-bound and swapping heavily has a different bottleneck entirely, and no amount of renicing addresses memory pressure or I/O wait.

items.stem: A user starts a long compilation with `make &` in their SSH session and disconnects without using `nohup`. Is the compilation process a daemon?

options.text: No — it is still attached to the terminal session and dies with it; a daemon has no controlling terminal at all
options.why: Backgrounding with `&` does not detach a process from its terminal session, which is exactly what distinguishes an ordinary background job from a daemon.

options.text: Yes, any process running in the background without an interactive prompt counts as a daemon
options.why: Not every background process is a daemon: this one is still attached to a terminal session and is typically killed when that session ends.

options.text: Yes, because it was started at the command line rather than by `systemctl` — how a process is started does not determine whether it is a daemon; what matters is whether it has detached from a controlling terminal
options.why: How a process is started does not determine whether it is a daemon; what matters is whether it has detached from a controlling terminal.

options.text: No, but only because `make` is a build tool rather than a long-running server
options.why: The distinction is about terminal attachment and lifetime, not about what category of program is running.

items.rationale: A daemon is a long-running background process with no controlling terminal, typically started at boot. A job merely backgrounded with `&` is still attached to its terminal session and, without `nohup` or `disown`, is usually killed when that session ends — it has not detached the way a daemon does.

items.stem: A program was written to detach itself from its terminal on startup — forking, calling `setsid()`, and re-parenting to PID 1 — but has no systemd unit file. Is it a daemon? Is it a service?

options.text: It is a daemon, because it has detached and runs in the background continuously; it is not a service, because nothing is supervising or restarting it
options.why: "Daemon" describes how the process runs, while "service" describes whether a management layer wraps it — this program has the first property but not the second.

options.text: It cannot be a daemon without a unit file, since daemons and services are the same thing under systemd
options.why: The two terms are not interchangeable: a program can detach itself perfectly well without any unit file, in which case it is a daemon but not a managed service.

options.text: It is both a daemon and a service, since any long-running background process qualifies as a service
options.why: A service specifically implies a supervision policy — starting, stopping, restarting — which this program has none of without a unit file.

options.text: It is neither, since only systemd-managed processes count as daemons on a modern distribution — the classic self-detaching pattern (fork, `setsid()`, re-parent to PID 1) is exactly what makes a process a daemon, with or without systemd managing it
options.why: The classic self-detaching pattern (fork, `setsid()`, re-parent to PID 1) is exactly what makes a process a daemon, with or without systemd managing it.

items.rationale: A daemon is defined by how it runs — detached from a terminal, long-lived — which this program achieves through the classic double-fork pattern. A service is a management layer on top of that, and without a unit file nothing restarts it or brings it back at boot, so it is a daemon without being a service.

items.stem: `ps` shows a process as `defunct`. What state is it in, and does sending it `kill -9` clear it?

options.text: It is a zombie — already exited, waiting for its parent to reap its status — and `kill -9` does nothing to it
options.why: A zombie is already dead and holds only a process-table entry; there is nothing left alive for a signal to act on.

options.text: It is an orphan whose parent has died, and `kill -9` forces it to exit properly — an orphan is still running and has simply been re-parented to PID 1; a `defunct` entry specifically describes a zombie, which has already exited
options.why: An orphan is still running and has simply been re-parented to PID 1; a `defunct` entry specifically describes a zombie, which has already exited.

options.text: It is a daemon that has lost its controlling terminal, and `kill -9` restarts it cleanly
options.why: A daemon that has detached from its terminal is running normally; `defunct` specifically marks a process that has already exited.

options.text: It is a process stuck in uninterruptible sleep, and `kill -9` will eventually succeed once I/O completes
options.why: Uninterruptible sleep is a different, still-alive state waiting on I/O; a `defunct` entry means the process has already exited.

items.rationale: A zombie has already exited but its parent has not yet read its exit status, so its process-table entry lingers, shown as `defunct` in `ps`. It consumes no CPU or memory and cannot be killed because it is already dead — the fix is to have the parent reap it, or wait for PID 1 to do so once the parent itself exits.

items.stem: A process launched by hand at the shell keeps dying, and nothing restarts it. The same program launched via a systemd unit restarts automatically after a crash. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: The unit wraps the process in a supervision policy — a service, as opposed to a bare process nobody is watching
options.why: A service adds restart behaviour, dependency ordering and boot-time activation on top of the process; a hand-launched process has none of that.

options.text: Nothing — a process and a service are the same object under two different names
options.why: The underlying program is identical either way; what differs is whether a management layer is watching and restarting it.

options.text: The systemd version must be running as a daemon while the hand-launched one is not
options.why: Both could equally detach from a terminal; the restart behaviour comes from the unit's `Restart=` policy, not from daemon status.

options.text: The hand-launched process was niced too low to be restarted automatically — a nice value affects CPU scheduling priority and has no bearing on whether anything restarts a process after it exits
options.why: A nice value affects CPU scheduling priority and has no bearing on whether anything restarts a process after it exits.

items.rationale: A service is a process wrapped in a management policy: how to start it, what to do when it exits, and whether it should come back at boot.
