A process launched by hand has none of that definition behind it, which is why only the unit-managed copy restarts itself. `systemctl` is the control interface for units and the manager that supplies that policy.

items.stem: A running application's configuration file has changed and it must pick up the change. Should an administrator run `systemctl restart app` or `systemctl reload app`?

options.text: `reload`, if the application supports it — it asks the running process to re-read its configuration without stopping it
options.why: `reload` tells the already-running process to re-read its own configuration in place, avoiding the interruption a stop-then-start restart causes.

options.text: `restart`, since it is always the safer choice regardless of what changed — avoids entirely for a configuration-only change
options.why: Restart stops and starts the process, causing an interruption that a reload — when supported — avoids entirely for a configuration-only change.

options.text: `systemctl daemon-reload`, since any configuration change requires reloading the manager
options.why: `daemon-reload` re-reads unit files, not an application's own configuration file; it would not make the running process notice the change at all.

options.text: `systemctl enable --now app`, to apply the new configuration at the next boot
options.why: Enabling changes only boot-time activation; it does not make the currently running process re-read anything right now.

items.rationale: `systemctl restart` stops and starts the process, while `systemctl reload` tells the already-running process to re-read its own configuration file — the appropriate choice when only the application's configuration, not the unit definition, has changed and the daemon supports reload.

items.stem: Someone says "systemd" and "`systemctl`" as if they were interchangeable. What is the actual relationship?

options.text: systemd is the manager process running as PID 1; `systemctl` is the client command used to control it
options.why: They are not the same object: one is the long-running manager, the other is the tool an administrator types commands into to talk to it.

options.text: They are two names for the same running process, used interchangeably by convention
options.why: Only systemd itself runs as PID 1; `systemctl` is a separate, short-lived command invoked each time it is run.

options.text: `systemctl` is the older SysV name for what became systemd — the older SysV-era mechanism is runlevels and `init`, not `systemctl`, which is a systemd-specific control command
options.why: The older SysV-era mechanism is runlevels and `init`, not `systemctl`, which is a systemd-specific control command.

options.text: systemd only manages boot; `systemctl` is the separate tool that manages running services
options.why: systemd itself supervises services throughout the machine's life, not only at boot; `systemctl` is simply how it is instructed either way.

items.rationale: systemd is the init system and service manager, running as PID 1 for the life of the machine. `systemctl` is the command-line client used to query and control it. Conflating the manager with the tool used to talk to it is a common but avoidable mix-up.

items.stem: `systemd-analyze blame` names a unit that took 40 seconds to initialise during a slow boot. Is that unit necessarily the cause of the slow boot?

options.text: Not necessarily — `blame` ranks duration, not delay; `systemd-analyze critical-chain` shows what actually held boot up
options.why: A slow unit that nothing else waits on can run fully in parallel and cost nothing, so duration alone does not identify the bottleneck.

options.text: Yes, the slowest unit in `blame`'s output is always what delayed the boot — because units start in parallel wherever dependencies allow, the slowest individual unit is not automatically the one that held up the critical path
options.why: Because units start in parallel wherever dependencies allow, the slowest individual unit is not automatically the one that held up the critical path.

options.text: No, because `blame` only measures time before the kernel finishes loading
options.why: `blame` measures each unit's own initialisation time during userspace startup, not a kernel-only phase.

options.text: No, because `blame` requires `daemon-reload` to be run first to produce accurate figures
options.why: `blame` reads recorded startup timing from the completed boot; it has no dependency on `daemon-reload` being run beforehand.

items.rationale: systemd activates units in parallel wherever the dependency graph allows, so `blame`'s ranking by duration does not show what was actually on the critical path. `systemd-analyze` alone reports the total boot time split by phase, and `systemd-analyze critical-chain` follows the ordering chain that determined when boot actually converged.

items.stem: An administrator wants to see the effective configuration of `nginx.service`, including any override applied through a drop-in file, rather than only the distribution-shipped definition. Which command shows that?

options.text: `systemctl cat nginx.service`, which prints the vendor unit plus every applicable drop-in, each labelled with its path
options.why: It is specifically designed to show what is actually in effect, including administrator overrides layered on top of the vendor-shipped file.

options.text: Reading `/usr/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service` directly is sufficient, since that is where the definitive file lives
options.why: That path holds only the distribution-shipped definition; an `/etc/systemd/system` override or a drop-in changing behaviour would not be visible there.

options.text: `systemctl list-units --type=service`, which lists every loaded service unit — that command lists which units are currently loaded, not the contents of one unit's effective configuration
options.why: That command lists which units are currently loaded, not the contents of one unit's effective configuration.

options.text: `systemctl daemon-reload`, which prints the current unit definitions as it reloads them
options.why: That command re-reads unit files and rebuilds the dependency graph; it does not print the unit's contents to the terminal.

items.rationale: `systemctl cat` prints the effective unit file plus every drop-in that applies to it, with each file's path shown as a comment — the way to see what is actually in effect rather than only the vendor-shipped definition under `/usr/lib/systemd/system`. `systemctl list-units` instead lists units currently loaded, not any single unit's file contents.

items.stem: A requirement states a service must both be running right now and still be running after every future reboot. Which single command satisfies both halves in one step?

options.text: `systemctl enable --now nginx`, enabling the boot-time symlink and starting it immediately in one step
options.why: It creates the boot-time symlink from the unit's `[Install]` section and starts the unit immediately, covering both halves of the requirement at once.

options.text: `systemctl start nginx` alone, since a successful start implies it will also come back after a reboot
options.why: Starting acts on the running system only and consults nothing about the next boot — a started-but-not-enabled service is simply absent after a reboot.

options.text: `systemctl enable nginx` alone, since enabling a unit also starts it immediately — `enable` only creates the boot-time symlink from `[Install]`; it does not touch the running system at all
options.why: `enable` only creates the boot-time symlink from `[Install]`; it does not touch the running system at all.

options.text: `systemctl daemon-reload nginx`, since reloading applies both the running and boot-time state
options.why: `daemon-reload` takes no unit argument and only re-reads unit files; it neither starts a unit nor changes its boot-time activation.

items.rationale: `systemctl start` and `systemctl enable` are orthogonal: one affects the running system now, the other affects the next boot, and neither implies the other. `systemctl enable --now` is exactly the shorthand for doing both in a single command.

items.stem: A service that was working fine for months is simply absent after an unrelated reboot — no crash, no error, nothing in the logs about it at all. What is the first command to run, and what does a result of `disabled` tell you?

options.text: `systemctl is-enabled <unit>`; a result of `disabled` is the entire explanation — the unit was configured and started by hand but never enabled
options.why: A unit that reports `disabled` was never going to survive a reboot regardless of how well it was running beforehand, since starting it never touches its boot-time state.

options.text: `systemctl is-active <unit>`, since an inactive result would explain why it is gone after reboot — checking whether it is active now says nothing about why it failed to come back; the boot-time question is answered by `is-enabled`, not `is-active`
options.why: Checking whether it is active now says nothing about why it failed to come back; the boot-time question is answered by `is-enabled`, not `is-active`.

options.text: `journalctl -u <unit> -b`, since a missing service always leaves an error explaining why it failed to start
options.why: A unit that was simply never enabled produces no failure at all — there is nothing in the logs to find, because the unit was never even asked to start.

options.text: `systemctl daemon-reload`, since re-reading unit files restores services that vanished after a reboot
options.why: Re-reading unit files has no bearing on whether a unit's boot-time symlink exists; it neither creates nor removes that state.

items.rationale: "The service is gone after a reboot" is diagnosed by checking `systemctl is-enabled <unit>` first. A reply of `disabled` fully explains the symptom: the service was started manually at some point and worked until the next reboot, at which point nothing pulled it back in because it was never enabled.

items.stem: A server needs to boot into a minimal, non-graphical state permanently from now on, not just for the next boot. Which command sets that as the standing default?

options.text: `systemctl set-default multi-user.target`, rewriting the standing default target
options.why: It changes where future boots converge by rewriting the `default.target` symlink, which is exactly a permanent, standing change.

options.text: `systemctl isolate multi-user.target`, since isolating a target makes it the new default
options.why: `isolate` only changes the running system right now; it does nothing about which target the next boot converges on.

options.text: `systemctl get-default multi-user.target`, since it sets the target it is given
options.why: `get-default` only reads and prints the current default; it takes no target argument to change anything.

options.text: `runlevel 3`, the SysV-era equivalent of the same request
options.why: `runlevel` only prints the previous and current SysV runlevel; it does not set anything, on this system or any other.

items.rationale: `default.target` is a symlink naming where boot converges, and `systemctl set-default` rewrites it — a change that persists across every future boot. `systemctl get-default` reads the current setting, and `isolate` changes the running system immediately but leaves the standing default untouched.

items.stem: To troubleshoot a graphical login failure right now, an administrator proposes `systemctl isolate rescue.target` on a production server that is currently serving traffic. What happens to units that `rescue.target` does not want?

options.text: They are stopped immediately, which is disruptive on a live production server and should be done deliberately, not casually
options.why: `isolate` starts what the named target wants and stops everything that is not part of it, right now, on the running system.

options.text: Nothing changes for them; `isolate` only affects graphical-session units — it stops every currently running unit that the named target does not want, which can include production services
options.why: `isolate` is not scoped to graphical units — it stops every currently running unit that the named target does not want, which can include production services.

options.text: They are only stopped after the next reboot, since `isolate` schedules rather than acts immediately
options.why: `isolate` acts on the running system immediately; it is `set-default` that only affects a future boot.

options.text: They are paused rather than stopped, and resume automatically once `default.target` is restored
options.why: `isolate` stops units outright rather than pausing them; nothing about the operation is reversible on its own.

items.rationale: `systemctl isolate` switches to a target immediately, starting what it wants and stopping every unit that is not part of it — on a running production server that stops real services, which is precisely why it is a disruptive command to reach for casually rather than the safer, non-immediate `set-default`.

items.stem: Under the systemd compatibility mapping, which target does SysV runlevel 5 correspond to, and which does runlevel 0 correspond to?

options.text: Runlevel 5 maps to `graphical.target`; runlevel 0 maps to `poweroff.target`
options.why: The documented mapping pairs 5 with a graphical login state and 0 with halting the machine, matching the SysV convention those numbers always had.

options.text: The pairing is reversed from that: `poweroff.target` is what 5 reaches, and `graphical.target` is what 0 reaches
options.why: This reverses the actual mapping — 0 has always meant halt, not a graphical login state, in both the SysV and systemd schemes.

options.text: Runlevel 5 and runlevel 0 both map to `multi-user.target`, since several runlevels collapse onto it
options.why: Runlevels 2, 3 and 4 collapse onto `multi-user.target`, but 5 and 0 each map to their own distinct target.

options.text: Neither maps to anything under systemd, since runlevels are not supported at all on modern systems
options.why: systemd documents an approximate compatibility mapping for every runlevel number rather than dropping support for the concept entirely.

items.rationale: systemd documents the mapping as 0 to `poweroff.target`, 1 to `rescue.target`, 2/3/4 to `multi-user.target`, 5 to `graphical.target`, and 6 to `reboot.target`. Because three runlevels collapse onto one target, the mapping loses information and cannot be reversed cleanly.

items.stem: Runlevels are described as mutually exclusive, but targets are not. What does that structural difference mean in practice?

options.text: Exactly one runlevel could be active at a time under SysV init, while several systemd targets can be active simultaneously
options.why: This is the structural reason the runlevel-to-target mapping loses information: a single exclusive state maps onto a set of targets that can coexist.

options.text: It means targets are simply renamed runlevels with no real behavioural difference
options.why: The mapping is explicitly approximate, not a rename, precisely because the exclusivity assumption behind runlevels does not hold for targets.

options.text: It means runlevels can be active simultaneously but targets cannot — this reverses the actual relationship; it is targets that compose and can be active together, not runlevels
options.why: This reverses the actual relationship; it is targets that compose and can be active together, not runlevels.

options.text: It means only `rescue.target` and `emergency.target` can coexist with other targets
options.why: Composability is not limited to those two special targets — `graphical.target` and `multi-user.target` coexist too, since one pulls in the other.

items.rationale: Runlevels were mutually exclusive under SysV init — the system was in exactly one at a time. Targets compose: `graphical.target` does not replace `multi-user.target`, it pulls it in, so several targets are active together. That is why the runlevel-to-target mapping is approximate rather than a straightforward rename. The `runlevel` command still prints the previous and current SysV runlevel on systems that track it.

items.stem: An administrator edits `nginx.service` to add `Restart=on-failure`, then runs `systemctl restart nginx`. The new restart policy does not appear to take effect. What is missing?

options.text: `systemctl daemon-reload` — until it runs, systemd is still acting on the unit definition it parsed earlier, not the edited file
options.why: A restart uses whatever definition the manager already has cached; only a reload makes it re-read the unit file from disk before the next activation.

options.text: Nothing is missing; `restart` always re-reads the unit file before restarting the process
options.why: A plain restart does not re-parse the unit file — that is specifically what `daemon-reload` does, and skipping it is the whole reason the edit appears to have no effect.

options.text: The change needed `systemctl reload nginx` instead of `restart` — `reload` asks the running nginx process to re-read its own application configuration; it has no bearing on systemd noticing a changed unit file
options.why: `reload` asks the running nginx process to re-read its own application configuration; it has no bearing on systemd noticing a changed unit file.

options.text: The unit needed `systemctl enable --now` run again to pick up the change
options.why: Re-enabling only recreates the boot-time symlink; it does not make the manager re-parse an edited unit file.

items.rationale: systemd caches parsed unit files, so editing one and then restarting the service still runs against the old cached definition. `systemctl daemon-reload` rescans the unit directories and rebuilds the dependency graph, and only after that does a restart pick up the change.

items.stem: Three similarly named operations exist: `systemctl daemon-reload`, `systemctl reload nginx`, and `systemctl restart nginx`. Which one re-reads unit files from disk, manager-wide?

options.text: `systemctl daemon-reload` — it takes no unit argument and rebuilds the dependency graph from every unit file
options.why: It is a manager-wide operation, unlike the other two, which each act on one named unit rather than on the set of unit definitions itself.

options.text: `systemctl reload nginx`, since "reload" is the word that implies re-reading configuration
options.why: That command asks the *nginx process itself* to re-read its own application configuration file — it does nothing to systemd's cached unit definitions.

options.text: `systemctl restart nginx`, since restarting naturally picks up whatever has changed
options.why: Restart stops and starts the process using whatever unit definition the manager already has cached; it does not re-parse the unit file.

options.text: All three do the same thing at different scopes, so any one of them suffices — not scoped variants of one action
options.why: They are three genuinely different operations — re-reading unit files, asking an application to reload, and stopping/starting a process — not scoped variants of one action.

items.rationale: `systemctl daemon-reload` takes no unit argument because it is a manager-wide operation: it re-reads every unit file and rebuilds the dependency graph. `reload <unit>` asks one running application to re-read its own configuration, and `restart <unit>` merely stops and starts the process — neither touches the cached unit definitions.

items.stem: A team installs a monitoring agent with the distribution's package manager, and separately runs `npm install express` inside one Node.js application. Are both operations installing "packages" in the same sense the exam means?

options.text: No — the monitoring agent is a system-wide OS package with dependency metadata read by the OS package manager; `npm install` resolves a library scoped to one application
options.why: The two share a word but differ in scope of ownership: one places distribution-owned software system-wide, the other resolves one project's own dependency manifest.

options.text: Yes, both are the same kind of package, just installed by different front-end commands — they differ in scope: an OS package is recorded in the system package database and owned by the distribution, while `npm` resolves libraries for one application only
options.why: They differ in scope: an OS package is recorded in the system package database and owned by the distribution, while `npm` resolves libraries for one application only.

options.text: No — the OS package came from a repository and the `npm` package did not come from anywhere at all
options.why: Both are fetched from somewhere; the distinguishing factor is scope (system-wide versus one application), not whether a remote source was involved.

options.text: Yes, and the difference only matters for which command performs the removal later — it is what the software is meant to serve and whose responsibility it is
options.why: The difference is more than a removal-command detail — it is what the software is meant to serve and whose responsibility it is.

Language package managers such as `npm`, `pip` and Maven resolve an application's own libraries instead, a distinct and narrower scope.

items.stem: What does installing a package register that a plain tarball copied into place by hand does not?

options.text: An entry in a local database recording which files belong to it, so the system can answer "who owns this file" or remove it cleanly later
