items.rationale: `/dev/null` discards data written to it and returns end-of-file immediately when read, while `/dev/zero` returns an endless stream of zero bytes on read — a common trap for anyone assuming `/dev/null` is a general-purpose discard for every use.

items.stem: A team plans to grow a filesystem while it stays mounted, and possibly shrink it later. Between ext4 and XFS, which choice keeps the shrink option open?

options.text: ext4 — it can be shrunk, though only while unmounted; XFS can be grown online but cannot be shrunk at all
options.why: The two filesystem types differ specifically in what resizing operations they support, and only ext4 supports shrinking under any circumstances.

options.text: XFS, since it is the more modern of the two and therefore supports every resize operation
options.why: Being more modern does not imply broader capability here — XFS specifically has no shrink support at all, online or offline.

options.text: Either — resizing capability is governed by the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, not by the filesystem type
options.why: Resize capability is a property of the on-disk format itself, which is exactly what filesystem type governs; the FHS says nothing about it.

options.text: Neither, since resizing any mounted Linux filesystem always requires reformatting first
options.why: ext4 supports shrinking without a full reformat, just not while mounted; reformatting is not the only route to a smaller filesystem.

items.rationale: Filesystem type determines resizing capability directly: XFS can be grown while mounted but cannot be shrunk at all, while ext4 can be shrunk, but only while unmounted. A plan that assumes "we will resize it later" is only safe once the type is known — created with `mkfs` and confirmed afterward with `blkid`.

items.stem: Files copied onto a USB stick formatted vFAT come back with different Unix ownership and permission bits than they had on the source filesystem. Is this a `chmod` failure?

options.text: No — vFAT stores no Unix ownership or permission bits at all, so what is shown afterward comes entirely from the mount options
options.why: Because the filesystem type itself has no concept of Unix ownership, whatever permissions appear are synthesised by the mount options rather than recovered from anything stored on disk.

options.text: Yes, `chmod` must have been run incorrectly before the files were copied — vFAT simply has no on-disk representation for ownership or permission bits to preserve in the first place
options.why: No `chmod` failure is required to produce this result — vFAT simply has no on-disk representation for ownership or permission bits to preserve in the first place.

options.text: No, but only because the FHS forbids storing permissions on removable media
options.why: The FHS governs directory layout and says nothing about what any given filesystem type can store; the limitation here is intrinsic to the vFAT format.

options.text: Yes, and re-running `chown` and `chmod` on the USB stick will make the change permanent
options.why: Because vFAT has nowhere to store Unix ownership, any such change would not persist across a remount either.

items.rationale: vFAT stores no Unix ownership or permission bits, so files copied onto it come back with whatever the mount options dictate rather than what they had on the source filesystem — a data-loss-looking surprise that is really a property of the destination filesystem type, not a `chmod` mistake.

items.stem: An administrator runs `mount /dev/sdb1 /srv/data`, but `/srv/data` already contained files. What happens to those pre-existing files?

options.text: They are hidden for as long as the mount lasts — not merged, and not deleted
options.why: Mounting attaches the new filesystem at that path, which obscures whatever was already there rather than combining or removing it; the original contents reappear once unmounted.

options.text: They are permanently deleted, since the mount overwrites the directory
options.why: Nothing is deleted — the original contents still exist on the underlying filesystem and reappear as soon as the mount is undone.

options.text: They are merged with the new filesystem's contents, showing both sets of files together
options.why: Mounting does not merge directory contents; it entirely obscures the mount point's previous contents for the duration of the mount.

options.text: Nothing changes, because a partition must be formatted before `mount` will do anything at all
options.why: `/dev/sdb1` is presumed already formatted here, and even if it were not, that would produce an error rather than leaving the pre-existing files visible.

items.rationale: Mounting attaches a filesystem into the tree at a chosen mount point. Any files that already existed at that path are hidden for as long as the mount lasts — neither merged nor deleted — and reappear once the filesystem is unmounted, which is the usual explanation for space or files that seem to have disappeared. `findmnt` reads the kernel's own view of what is currently mounted, rather than `/etc/fstab`'s stated intent.

items.stem: `umount /mnt/data` fails with "target is busy." What is the correct next step, as opposed to reaching for `umount -l`?

options.text: Use `lsof` or `fuser` to find the process holding the filesystem open, and stop or redirect it before unmounting
options.why: A busy target means some process still has a file open there or has its working directory inside it; finding and addressing that process resolves the cause rather than papering over it.

options.text: `umount -l` is always the correct fix for a busy target, since it forces the unmount immediately
options.why: Using `-l` to force past a busy filesystem papers over the problem rather than finding the offending process, and is specifically flagged as the wrong habit to reach for first.

options.text: Reformat the filesystem, since "busy" indicates it is corrupted — a busy target is a normal, expected condition caused by an open file handle or a working directory inside the mount; it says nothing about corruption
options.why: A busy target is a normal, expected condition caused by an open file handle or a working directory inside the mount; it says nothing about corruption.

options.text: Reboot the machine, since a busy mount cannot be resolved without a restart
options.why: Identifying and stopping the process holding the mount open resolves this without any reboot being necessary.

items.rationale: `umount` fails with "target is busy" while any process holds a file open on that filesystem or has its working directory inside it. `lsof` or `fuser` names the offending process, which should be addressed directly rather than using `-l` (lazy unmount) to paper over the underlying cause.

items.stem: List the six whitespace-separated fields of an `/etc/fstab` line, in order.

options.text: Device, mount point, filesystem type, mount options, dump flag, and fsck pass order
options.why: Each line names what to mount, where, in what format, with what options, and how the two remaining maintenance flags should treat it.

options.text: Device, mount point, mount options, filesystem type, dump flag, and fsck pass order
options.why: This swaps the third and fourth fields — filesystem type comes before mount options, not after.

options.text: Device, mount point, filesystem type, owner, group, and permissions
options.why: An fstab line does not record ownership or permission bits at all; the fifth and sixth fields are the dump flag and the fsck pass order.

options.text: UUID, label, device, mount point, options, and fsck pass order
options.why: UUID and label are alternative ways of naming the first field (the device), not two separate fields of their own.

items.rationale: `/etc/fstab` has six positional, unlabelled fields in order: device, mount point, filesystem type, mount options, dump flag, and fsck pass order. Because the fields are positional, a missing options field silently shifts the two numeric fields that follow it.

items.stem: An `/etc/fstab` entry was just added for a new filesystem. What is the safe way to confirm the line is correct before the next reboot depends on it?

options.text: `mount -a`, which mounts everything in the file not marked `noauto` and surfaces a syntax error while a shell is still available
options.why: It applies the fstab file to the running system immediately, which is exactly how to catch a mistake while it is still easy to fix rather than at boot time.

options.text: Nothing is needed; a malformed `/etc/fstab` entry is safely ignored at boot
options.why: A malformed entry does not fail quietly — it can leave systemd waiting on a device that is never found and dropping into emergency mode at the next boot.

options.text: `findmnt --target`, which shows what is currently mounted at the intended path
options.why: That command reports the running kernel's current mount table, not whether the newly written fstab line itself is syntactically valid.

options.text: `blkid`, to regenerate the UUID for the new filesystem before rebooting — `blkid` reports the type, UUID and label of a filesystem; it does not validate or apply an fstab entry
options.why: `blkid` reports the type, UUID and label of a filesystem; it does not validate or apply an fstab entry.

items.rationale: A malformed or wrong `/etc/fstab` entry can leave the boot process waiting on a device that cannot be found and dropping into emergency mode. `mount -a` applies the file to the running system immediately, surfacing any error while a working shell is still available to fix it.

items.stem: A disk uses the older MBR partitioning scheme. What are its two defining limits compared with GPT?

options.text: At most four primary partitions, and a maximum disk size of roughly 2 TiB
options.why: Both limits come from the fixed-size 512-byte structure MBR uses to record the partition table, which GPT was designed to remove.

options.text: At most four partitions total, including logical ones, and no maximum disk size at all
options.why: One of MBR's four primary slots can hold an extended partition containing further logical partitions, and MBR does impose a roughly 2 TiB size ceiling.

options.text: No limit on partition count, but a maximum disk size of roughly 2 TiB
options.why: MBR does cap primary partitions at four; the count limit is real, not absent.

options.text: At most four primary partitions, with no size limit, since size limits belong to the filesystem type rather than the partition table
options.why: The 2 TiB ceiling is a property of the MBR partition table format itself, independent of whatever filesystem type is later created on a partition.

items.rationale: MBR is limited to four primary partitions (one of which can be an extended partition holding further logical ones) and to disks of roughly 2 TiB, both consequences of its fixed, small on-disk structure. GPT, the UEFI-era replacement, removes both limits.

items.stem: `lsblk` shows a disk and `df -h` shows nothing for it at all, though `fdisk -l` confirms a partition exists on it. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The partition has no filesystem on it yet — it is invisible to `df` and cannot be mounted until formatted
options.why: A partition is only a region of space; `df` reports on mounted filesystems, and an unformatted partition has neither a filesystem nor a mount to report.

options.text: The partition table must be corrupted, since a real partition should always appear in `df`
options.why: `fdisk -l` already confirms the partition table is intact and the partition exists; the missing piece is a filesystem, not a corrupted table.

options.text: The partition is mounted read-only, which hides it from `df -h` — a read-only mount still appears in `df -h`, showing its usage; the described symptom is a total absence, consistent with no filesystem existing at all
options.why: A read-only mount still appears in `df -h`, showing its usage; the described symptom is a total absence, consistent with no filesystem existing at all.

options.text: `lsblk` and `fdisk -l` are reporting on two different disks by coincidence
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests two different disks; the simpler and standard explanation is an unformatted partition.

items.rationale: A partition with no filesystem on it is invisible to `df` and cannot be mounted, so "the disk does not show up" in `df` while `lsblk` and `fdisk -l` confirm the partition exists often means simply that it was never formatted with `mkfs`.

items.stem: `df -h` reports a filesystem is only half full, but creating a new file on it fails with "No space left on device." What should be checked next, and why?

options.text: `df -i`, since the filesystem may have exhausted its inode table while data blocks remain free
options.why: A filesystem full of tiny files can run out of inodes long before it runs out of data blocks, and that exhaustion is invisible to a plain `df -h` block-usage report.

options.text: Nothing further is needed; `df -h` already proves there is no real problem and the error is spurious
options.why: The error is real — it just is not about blocks. Inode exhaustion is a distinct, common cause that block-usage figures alone cannot reveal.

options.text: `du -sh`, to find which directory is consuming the most space
options.why: `du` totals file sizes, which is the wrong lens when the filesystem still has free space by that measure; the symptom described points at the inode table instead.

options.text: `ls -i`, to confirm two files are not accidentally hard-linked together
options.why: Checking for shared inodes between two specific files does not explain a filesystem-wide inability to create any new file.

items.rationale: The number of inodes on a filesystem is normally fixed at creation time, so a filesystem holding many tiny files can exhaust its inode table while gigabytes of data blocks remain free. `df -i` reports inode usage directly, and it is the standard next check when `df -h` shows space but writes still fail.

items.stem: Two directory entries have the same size, the same modification time, and the same content. What single check confirms they are actually the same file rather than two coincidentally identical copies?

options.text: Comparing their inode numbers with `ls -i` — the same number means the same underlying file
options.why: The inode number is the identity of the file itself; two names sharing one number are definitively the same file, not merely similar copies.

options.text: Comparing their filenames, since identical filenames always indicate the same underlying file
options.why: A filename is only a directory entry pointing at an inode; two different files in different directories can easily share a name without being the same file.

options.text: Comparing their permission bits with `ls -l`, since identical permissions confirm identity
options.why: Two entirely separate files can easily share identical permission bits by coincidence; that says nothing about whether they are the same underlying file.

options.text: Comparing their paths with `findmnt`, since files on the same filesystem must be identical if their paths resolve similarly
options.why: `findmnt` reports on mounted filesystems, not on individual file identity, and nothing about path similarity establishes that two entries share an inode.

items.rationale: The inode holds everything the filesystem knows about a file except its name; a directory entry is just a mapping from a name to an inode number. Two names sharing the same inode number, as reported by `ls -i`, are provably the same file rather than two files that merely look alike.

items.stem: A file has one hard link and one symbolic link pointing at it. The hard-linked name is deleted. What happens to the file's data, and what happens to the symlink?

options.text: The data survives, since the inode's link count merely drops by one; the symlink still resolves through the surviving name
options.why: A hard link is just another name for the same inode, so removing one name does not touch the data as long as another name (or the symlink's target) still exists.

options.text: The data is deleted immediately, and the symlink becomes dangling — deleting one of several hard-linked names only decrements the link count; the underlying data is freed only once the count reaches zero and nothing has it open
options.why: Deleting one of several hard-linked names only decrements the link count; the underlying data is freed only once the count reaches zero and nothing has it open.

options.text: The data survives, but the symlink is automatically updated to point at the remaining name
options.why: A symlink stores a fixed path string; nothing about deleting a hard link causes the symlink's stored target to be rewritten.

options.text: Both the data and the symlink are deleted together, since they share the same inode
options.why: A symlink has its own separate inode holding a path string; it does not share an inode with the file it points to.

items.rationale: A hard link is an additional directory entry pointing at an existing inode, so deleting one name only decrements that inode's link count; the data survives as long as the count has not reached zero. The symlink, holding its own separate path, keeps working through whichever original name still resolves.

items.stem: A backup script tries `ln /data/report.csv /backup/report.csv` across two different mounted filesystems, and it fails. Switching to `ln -s` succeeds. Why the difference?

options.text: A hard link refers to an inode number, meaningful only within one filesystem, so it cannot cross a filesystem boundary; a symlink stores a path and has no such restriction
options.why: Because inode numbers are only unique within a single filesystem, `ln` refuses to create a hard link across two different ones, while `ln -s` simply stores a path string that works regardless.

options.text: `ln` is simply broken for this use case and `ln -s` should always be preferred instead
options.why: `ln` works correctly within a single filesystem; the failure here is specifically the cross-filesystem restriction, not a general defect.

options.text: The destination directory must not have existed yet, which only `ln -s` tolerates
options.why: Nothing in the scenario indicates a missing destination directory; the described failure is the standard cross-filesystem restriction on hard links.

options.text: `/backup` must be a read-only mount, which blocks `ln` but not `ln -s` — a read-only destination would block both kinds of link creation equally; the actual restriction described is specific to hard links crossing filesystems
options.why: A read-only destination would block both kinds of link creation equally; the actual restriction described is specific to hard links crossing filesystems.

items.rationale: A hard link is a reference to an inode number, and inode numbers are meaningful only within one filesystem, so `ln` refuses to create one across a filesystem boundary. A symbolic link stores a path string instead and has no such restriction, which is why `ln -s` succeeds where `ln` does not.

items.stem: `df -h` reports a filesystem at 100% used, but `du -sh` walking the same filesystem from the top totals far less than what `df` reports. What kind of cause does that gap point at?

options.text: A structural cause invisible to `du` — most commonly a deleted file still held open by a running process
options.why: A deleted-but-open file keeps its blocks allocated on the filesystem, but has no name left for `du` to walk to, so it never appears in the total.

options.text: `du` must simply be miscounting, and rerunning it with different flags will resolve the discrepancy
options.why: `du` is not miscounting; it fundamentally cannot see certain categories of space, such as a deleted-but-open file, regardless of which flags are used.

options.text: The filesystem must have run out of inodes rather than blocks — inode exhaustion produces "No space left on device" on new writes even with free blocks; it does not explain a large gap between reported used space and a directory walk's total
options.why: Inode exhaustion produces "No space left on device" on new writes even with free blocks; it does not explain a large gap between reported used space and a directory walk's total.

options.text: The discrepancy always means the filesystem needs an `fsck` before anything else is checked
options.why: A structural check is not the standard first response to this specific symptom; `df` and `du` disagreeing has well-known, non-corruption causes to check first.

items.rationale: `df` reports what the filesystem itself has allocated, which includes blocks belonging to files that have been unlinked but are still held open by a running process; `du` walks directory names and cannot see such a file at all, since it has no name left to walk to. That is the classic explanation when `du`'s total falls well short of `df`'s.

items.stem: A filesystem reports full. Walk through the correct diagnostic order: what is checked first, second, and third?

options.text: `df -h` to find which filesystem is full, then `df -i` to rule out inode exhaustion, then `du -sh` descending from the mount point to locate the largest tree
options.why: Working outward from the cheapest check identifies which filesystem, then which resource (blocks or inodes), then which directory is actually responsible.

options.text: `du -sh /` immediately, since it directly finds the largest files on the whole machine in one pass
options.why: Running `du` over the entire machine first skips identifying which filesystem is actually affected and wastes time walking filesystems that are not the problem.

options.text: `lsof +L1` first, since deleted-but-open files are always the cause of a full filesystem — deleted-but-open files are one possible cause, not the only one, and checking for them before confirming which filesystem and which resource is full is out of order
options.why: Deleted-but-open files are one possible cause, not the only one, and checking for them before confirming which filesystem and which resource is full is out of order.

options.text: `fsck` immediately, since a full filesystem should always be checked for structural damage first
options.why: A full filesystem is not itself evidence of corruption, and running `fsck` first skips the cheap checks that usually explain the symptom directly.

items.rationale: The efficient order works outward from the cheapest check: `df -h` identifies which filesystem is full, `df -i` on that filesystem rules in or out inode exhaustion, and only then does `du -sh` descending from the mount point locate the specific directory responsible — checking the three structural causes (unlinked-open file, hidden mount, reserved blocks) if `du`'s total still falls short.

items.stem: `free -h` shows several gigabytes of swap in use on a server that otherwise seems healthy. Is that, by itself, evidence of a memory problem?

options.text: No — swap in use and swapping in progress are different things; pages evicted hours ago and never touched since remain "used" without indicating current trouble
options.why: A non-zero swap-used figure only shows that some memory was paged out at some point; the actual warning sign is a high current rate of swap-in and swap-out.

options.text: Yes, any non-zero swap usage means the machine needs more RAM immediately
options.why: Some swap usage is normal — the kernel pages out genuinely idle memory to free RAM for cache — and does not by itself indicate a shortage.

options.text: No, but only because `free -h` cannot report swap usage accurately — `free -h` reports swap usage accurately; the issue is how to interpret a non-zero figure, not the accuracy of the tool
options.why: `free -h` reports swap usage accurately; the issue is how to interpret a non-zero figure, not the accuracy of the tool.

options.text: Yes, and disabling swap entirely is the correct fix for a machine under any memory pressure
options.why: Disabling swap does not remove memory pressure; it converts a slow, swapping system into one where the kernel's out-of-memory killer terminates a process instead.

items.rationale: Swap usage is a diagnostic signal that is easy to misread. Some swap in use is normal, since the kernel evicts genuinely idle pages to free RAM for cache; what actually indicates trouble is a high rate of swap-in and swap-out happening now, which `free`'s repeated sampling (`-s`) shows better than a single snapshot.

items.stem: A newly created swap partition has been prepared but `swapon --show` lists nothing active, and `swapon /dev/sdb2` reports an error. What step was most likely skipped?

options.text: `mkswap` was never run on the device, so it has no swap signature for `swapon` to activate
options.why: `swapon` activates an area that has already been prepared as swap; without that preparation step there is nothing valid for it to turn on.

options.text: The partition needs to be formatted with `mkfs -t ext4` before it can be used as swap
options.why: Swap space is not a regular filesystem and is not created with `mkfs`; it is prepared specifically with `mkswap`.

options.text: An `/etc/fstab` entry must exist before `swapon` will activate any device at all
options.why: A device can be activated directly with `swapon <device>` without any fstab entry; the entry is only needed for it to activate automatically at boot.

options.text: The partition must first be added to a volume group before it can hold swap — swap can be created directly on a plain partition; involvement of a volume group is unrelated to whether `swapon` can activate it
options.why: Swap can be created directly on a plain partition; involvement of a volume group is unrelated to whether `swapon` can activate it.

items.rationale: Swap space is created with `mkswap`, which writes the signature `swapon` looks for, and only then activated with `swapon`. Running `swapon` on a partition that was never prepared with `mkswap` fails because there is no swap signature there for it to recognise.

items.stem: What advantage does an LVM logical volume have over a plain disk partition, which is the reason it is worth recognising for this exam?

options.text: It can be resized and can span more than one physical disk, which a plain partition cannot do
options.why: Pooling physical volumes into a volume group and carving logical volumes out of that pool is exactly what lets a volume grow, shrink or move across devices.

options.text: It is faster than a plain partition for every kind of workload — lVM adds a layer of abstraction for flexibility; it does not inherently make storage faster, and speed is not the property being tested here
options.why: LVM adds a layer of abstraction for flexibility; it does not inherently make storage faster, and speed is not the property being tested here.

options.text: It automatically protects data against drive failure, the way RAID does
options.why: Redundancy against drive failure is what RAID provides; LVM by itself is about flexible sizing and pooling, not fault tolerance.

options.text: It removes the need for a filesystem to be created on top of it
options.why: A logical volume still needs a filesystem created on it with `mkfs`, exactly like a plain partition would.

items.rationale: LVM pools physical volumes into a volume group, from which logical volumes are carved out. Its one selling point over a bare partition is that a logical volume can later be grown, shrunk, or moved across several physical disks — recognition of that three-layer vocabulary (PV, VG, LV) is the LFCA-level expectation, summarised respectively by `pvs`, `vgs` and `lvs`.

items.stem: A system needs to survive the loss of any one drive while maximising usable capacity from four drives. Which RAID level fits, and how many drives does it need at minimum?

options.text: RAID 5, needing at least three drives and giving the capacity of all but one
options.why: RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity, surviving exactly one drive failure while sacrificing only one drive's worth of capacity to redundancy.

options.text: RAID 0, since striping across four drives gives the largest usable capacity of any option
options.why: RAID 0 has no redundancy at all and loses everything if any single drive fails — it does not survive a drive loss, which the requirement specifically asks for.

options.text: RAID 1, since mirroring is the simplest way to survive a drive failure
options.why: RAID 1 survives a drive loss but gives only the capacity of one drive regardless of how many are mirrored, which does not maximise usable capacity from four drives.

options.text: RAID 10, needing at least four drives and giving the same usable capacity as RAID 5
options.why: RAID 10 needs at least four drives, correctly, but gives only half the raw capacity, which is less than RAID 5's all-but-one — it does not maximise capacity here.

items.rationale: RAID 5 needs at least three drives, gives the capacity of all but one, and survives exactly one drive failure — the best capacity-to-redundancy trade-off of the options for surviving a single drive loss. RAID 6, RAID 10 and RAID 1 all trade away more capacity for additional protection.

items.stem: A team relies on a mirrored RAID 1 array and treats it as their backup strategy. An operator accidentally deletes a critical directory. What does the mirror do?

options.text: It faithfully mirrors the deletion to the second drive just as quickly as any other write, so RAID alone does not recover the directory
options.why: RAID protects against a drive failing; it applies every write, including a deletion, to both members with equal fidelity, which is exactly why it is not a substitute for a backup.

options.text: It protects the directory, since RAID 1 keeps an independent copy of the data by design — the second drive is kept in lockstep with the first rather than independent of it, so the "protection" a backup provides against deletion is not what mirroring gives
options.why: The second drive is kept in lockstep with the first rather than independent of it, so the "protection" a backup provides against deletion is not what mirroring gives.

options.text: It automatically preserves a prior version of the directory before the deletion, since mirrors are point-in-time
options.why: A mirror is continuously kept current with the primary, not captured at a point in time, so there is no earlier version retained anywhere in the array.

options.text: It depends on which RAID controller is used, since some controllers block destructive commands
options.why: RAID operates below the filesystem, mirroring whatever writes the operating system issues; it has no awareness of whether a given write is destructive.

items.rationale: RAID protects only against a drive failing — not against accidental deletion, corruption, or any other destructive write, all of which are mirrored or parity-protected just as faithfully as a legitimate write. That is why RAID levels are never a substitute for backups.

items.stem: A user wants to edit their personal crontab. Why is `crontab -e` preferred over opening the spool file under `/var/spool/cron/` directly in a text editor?

options.text: `crontab -e` validates the syntax before installing the result and ensures the daemon notices the change
options.why: Editing the spool file directly can leave the daemon unaware of the edit and bypasses the syntax check the command performs before installing anything.

options.text: There is no real difference; both approaches update the same file identically
options.why: The command path adds a validation step and guarantees the daemon picks up the change, neither of which a direct file edit provides.

options.text: Editing the spool file is preferred, since `crontab -e` only works for system crontabs, not personal ones
options.why: `crontab -e` is specifically the personal crontab editor; system crontabs under `/etc/cron.d/` are a different, separate mechanism.

options.text: `crontab -e` is required because personal crontabs cannot contain more than one line
options.why: A personal crontab can hold any number of lines; the reason to prefer the command is validation and daemon notification, not a line-count restriction.

items.rationale: A user crontab is edited through `crontab -e` because the command validates the syntax and installs the result into the spool directory the daemon watches. Editing the spool file directly can leave cron unaware of the change and skips the validation step entirely.

items.stem: A laptop was powered off overnight, missing its scheduled 03:00 cron job entirely; the job never ran once the machine came back on. Is plain cron broken?

options.text: No — cron simply skips a scheduled time that passes while the machine is off; `anacron` exists specifically to compensate for that
options.why: Cron has no memory of a missed schedule window; catching up on a run missed while powered off is a separate mechanism cron does not provide by itself.

options.text: Yes, cron should always run a missed job as soon as the machine powers back on
options.why: That catch-up behaviour is exactly what plain cron lacks and what `anacron` was built to add — expecting it from cron itself is the mistake here.

options.text: No, but the job must have been accidentally removed with `crontab -r` — nothing in the scenario suggests the crontab was removed; a missed run on a machine that was off is the far more direct and standard explanation
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests the crontab was removed; a missed run on a machine that was off is the far more direct and standard explanation.

options.text: Yes, and the fix is to switch the job to a `.timer` unit without `Persistent=true`
options.why: A timer without `Persistent=true` would show exactly the same behaviour as cron here; the catch-up property requires that setting specifically.

items.rationale: Cron simply skips a scheduled time that passes while the machine is powered off — it is not a fault. `anacron` exists to compensate for that on machines that are not on continuously, and a systemd timer with `Persistent=true` is the equivalent modern alternative. `crontab -l` would have confirmed the job was still scheduled all along.

items.stem: A crontab line reads `30 4 1,15 * 5 /usr/local/bin/report.sh`. Both the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted. When does the job actually run?

options.text: At 04:30 on the 1st and 15th of every month, and additionally at 04:30 every Friday
options.why: When both day fields are restricted, they combine with OR rather than AND, so either condition being satisfied triggers the run.

options.text: At 04:30, only on whichever day is both the 1st or 15th of the month and a Friday
options.why: The two day fields do not combine with AND; treating them that way would make the job run far less often than the five-field syntax specifies.

options.text: At 04:30 on the 1st and 15th of every month only; the day-of-week field is ignored when the day-of-month field is also set
options.why: Neither day field is ever silently ignored — when both are restricted, both take effect and combine with OR.

options.text: At 04:30 every Friday only; the day-of-month field is ignored when the day-of-week field is also set
options.why: Both restricted day fields take effect together via OR; the day-of-month field is not overridden by the day-of-week field.

items.rationale: When both the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted (neither is `*`), cron combines them with OR rather than AND: the command runs when either matches. `30 4 1,15 * 5` therefore runs at 04:30 on the 1st and 15th and every Friday — a genuinely counter-intuitive rule worth memorising precisely. Entries like this are installed through `crontab -e`.

items.stem: A crontab entry runs `backup.sh` (a bare command name, no path) and works perfectly when typed by hand at the shell, but silently does nothing on schedule. What is the standard diagnostic first step, and what is usually wrong?

options.text: Assume the environment: cron does not source shell startup files and supplies a minimal `PATH`, so a bare command name is often not found
options.why: Cron sets `SHELL` to `/bin/sh`, takes `HOME` and `LOGNAME` from the account's `/etc/passwd` row, and never sources `~/.bashrc` or `/etc/profile`, so a bare name resolved by an interactive shell's `PATH` may not resolve at all under cron.

options.text: The crontab syntax must contain a typo in one of the five time fields
options.why: A typo in the time fields would produce a run at the wrong time or not at all in a way distinguishable from this, but the described symptom — total silence with no output — is the signature of the sparse cron environment, not a scheduling error.

options.text: The job must have been removed by an accidental `crontab -r` — if the crontab had been removed, `crontab -l` would show it missing entirely; the scenario describes the entry running silently on schedule with no visible effect
options.why: If the crontab had been removed, `crontab -l` would show it missing entirely; the scenario describes the entry running silently on schedule with no visible effect.

options.text: cron jobs cannot execute shell scripts at all, only single binaries
options.why: Cron happily executes shell scripts; the actual obstacle here is that the bare command name cannot be found under cron's minimal `PATH`.

items.rationale: The environment a cron job runs in is not the interactive shell's: cron sets a short default `PATH`, does not source `~/.bashrc` or `/etc/profile`, and takes `HOME`/`LOGNAME` from `/etc/passwd`. A bare command name that resolves fine interactively is the classic case that fails silently under cron; the fix is an absolute path or an explicit `PATH=` line in the crontab.

items.stem: An administrator enables `backup.service` directly, expecting it to run on a schedule the way a cron job would. What actually happens?

options.text: The service starts at every boot, which is not a schedule at all; the `.timer` unit is what needed to be enabled instead
options.why: A timer and its paired service are separate units, and enabling the service on its own only activates it at boot rather than on the timer's intended schedule.

options.text: The service runs on the schedule defined by `OnCalendar=` in the paired `.timer` unit, since they are linked automatically
options.why: Enabling the service does not consult the timer's schedule at all; only enabling the `.timer` unit itself causes activation on that schedule.

options.text: Nothing happens, since `.service` units cannot be enabled without a crontab entry pointing at them
options.why: A `.service` unit can be enabled on its own perfectly well; the issue is that doing so only activates it at boot, not on any recurring schedule.

options.text: The service is rejected by `systemctl` because it has no `OnCalendar=` directive of its own
options.why: `OnCalendar=` belongs to the `.timer` unit, not the `.service` unit; a service unit is not expected to carry that directive and enabling it does not fail for lacking one.

items.rationale: A timer unit is paired by name with a service unit it activates on a schedule. Enabling the service instead of the timer is the standard mistake: it makes the job run at every boot, which is not a schedule — the timer, not the service, is what must be enabled to get scheduled activation. `systemctl list-timers` shows every timer with its next and last activation.

items.stem: Name two advantages a systemd timer has over plain cron for a scheduled job.

options.text: Output is captured in the queryable journal rather than mailed, and a missed run can be made up with `Persistent=true`
options.why: Both are direct consequences of a timer activating a fully-fledged systemd service rather than handing a command straight to a shell the way cron does.

options.text: Timers are simpler to write than crontab lines, and they require no separate unit file
options.why: A timer requires a separate `.timer` unit paired with a `.service` unit — genuinely more moving parts than a single crontab line, not fewer.

options.text: Timers run with a full interactive shell environment, unlike cron — a full interactive environment is not one of them
options.why: The examinable advantages are journal logging, dependency handling and catch-up behaviour — a full interactive environment is not one of them.

options.text: Timers can run system-wide scripts, while cron is restricted to per-user jobs only — system-wide scheduled jobs exist under plain cron too, via `/etc/crontab` and `/etc/cron.d/`; that is not a capability unique to timers
options.why: System-wide scheduled jobs exist under plain cron too, via `/etc/crontab` and `/etc/cron.d/`; that is not a capability unique to timers.

items.rationale: Because a timer activates a real systemd service rather than handing a command to a shell, it inherits the manager's features automatically: output captured in the journal (queryable with `journalctl -u`), full dependency ordering, and — with `Persistent=true` — the ability to catch up on a run missed while the machine was off.

items.stem: An administrator is following a live tail of a busy log with `tail -f` when the log gets rotated by `logrotate` and renamed aside. New entries stop appearing. Which command survives rotation, and why?

options.text: `tail -F`, because it follows the file by name and reopens it after a rename, rather than staying attached to the old inode
options.why: `-f` keeps holding the original file descriptor, which now points at the renamed, no-longer-growing file; `-F` notices the name has a fresh file and reopens it.

options.text: `tail -f` should already handle rotation correctly, since it is designed to follow a growing log
options.why: `-f` stays with the original inode it opened, which is exactly what stops updating the moment the log is rotated away under a new name.

options.text: `less +F`, since only `less` supports following a log across rotation — `less +F` follows similarly to `tail -f` and shares the same limitation; the option that specifically reopens by name is `tail -F`
options.why: `less +F` follows similarly to `tail -f` and shares the same limitation; the option that specifically reopens by name is `tail -F`.

options.text: Neither survives rotation; the session must be restarted manually every time a log rotates
options.why: `tail -F` is specifically designed to survive rotation by reopening the file under its name, so a manual restart is not required.

items.rationale: `tail -f` follows the specific file descriptor it opened, which after rotation still points at the old, now-static file under its renamed path. `tail -F` follows the *name* instead, reopening the newly created file once rotation replaces it — the option that keeps working across a rotation.

items.stem: A filter is set to capture severity level 3 (Error) and above. Does it also capture Warning-level messages?

options.text: No — severity 3 and above means levels 3, 2, 1 and 0, and Warning is level 4, a less severe level than 3
options.why: The scale runs opposite to intuition: the most severe level has the lowest number, so "level 3 and above" means numerically lower, more severe levels only.

options.text: Yes, "level 3 and above" naturally includes Warning since it feels like a lesser problem than Error
options.why: Numerically, Warning (4) is a higher number than Error (3), and on this inverted scale a higher number is less severe, so it falls outside the filter.

options.text: It depends on the facility the message was logged under, not the severity level — facility identifies the source subsystem and is a separate dimension from severity; it does not change whether a given severity number is captured by this filter
options.why: Facility identifies the source subsystem and is a separate dimension from severity; it does not change whether a given severity number is captured by this filter.

options.text: Yes, because syslog severities count upward from least to most severe starting at 1
options.why: The scale starts at 0 for Emergency, the most severe level, and counts upward toward less severe levels, the opposite of what this option describes.

items.rationale: Syslog severity runs from Emergency (0) as most severe down to Debug (7) as least severe — the numbering is inverted from intuition. Filtering to "level 3 and above" in severity means 3, 2, 1 and 0 (Error through Emergency), which does not include Warning at level 4.

items.stem: A badly behaved application logs routine, harmless status messages at Error severity. What is the consequence for a monitoring filter tuned to alert on Error and above?

options.text: It floods the filter with false alarms, because severity is a claim by the emitting program, not an assessment by the logging system
options.why: The logging system has no way to second-guess the severity a program chooses to attach to its own messages, so a badly calibrated emitter degrades any filter built on that scale.

options.text: Nothing changes, since the logging system automatically re-classifies mislabelled messages — no such automatic re-classification happens; the logging system records whatever severity the emitting program attaches to a message
options.why: No such automatic re-classification happens; the logging system records whatever severity the emitting program attaches to a message.

options.text: The messages are silently dropped, since Error severity from a non-critical process is filtered out by default
options.why: There is no default behaviour that drops messages based on which process emitted them; the messages pass through at the severity the application chose.

options.text: The facility field automatically corrects the severity based on which subsystem is logging
options.why: Facility identifies the source subsystem and is independent of severity; it does not adjust or override the severity a message carries.

items.rationale: Severity is set by whichever program emits the message, not assessed independently by the logging system. A badly behaved application logging routine chatter at Error level floods any filter tuned to catch real problems at that severity, since the system has no mechanism to override the emitter's own claim.

items.stem: After a crash, `journalctl -b -1` returns nothing at all, as if the previous boot never happened. What is the most likely explanation, and what confirms it?

options.text: The journal is volatile: without `/var/log/journal` existing, it lives under `/run` and is discarded at every reboot; `journalctl --list-boots` confirms what is retained
options.why: By default the journal is persistent only if `/var/log/journal` exists; otherwise it is memory-backed and vanishes at the very reboot that would otherwise let it be inspected.

options.text: `journalctl` itself must be malfunctioning, since a crash should always leave some trace
options.why: The tool is working correctly; an empty result for the previous boot is the expected behaviour of a volatile, non-persistent journal, not a fault in `journalctl`.

options.text: The messages must be in `/var/log/syslog` instead, since journald never captures kernel or crash messages
options.why: journald does capture kernel and crash-time messages when persistent storage exists; the issue here is that persistence was never configured at all.

options.text: `-b -1` is the wrong syntax and should instead be `-b 1` to see the previous boot — `-b -1` is the correct syntax for the boot before the current one; the empty result is a persistence problem, not a syntax error
options.why: `-b -1` is the correct syntax for the boot before the current one; the empty result is a persistence problem, not a syntax error.

items.rationale: The journal is persistent only if `/var/log/journal` exists; otherwise it lives in `/run/log/journal`, which is memory-backed and discarded at every reboot. `journalctl --list-boots` shows what is actually retained, and if nothing is, that absence is itself the finding — enabling persistent storage is the first remediation.

items.stem: A service will not start. What is the diagnostic order across `systemctl status`, `journalctl -u <unit> -b`, and `journalctl -p err -b`?

options.text: `systemctl status <unit>` for the last few lines and exit status, then `journalctl -u <unit> -b` for everything that unit logged this boot, then `journalctl -p err -b` to widen the search to any failing dependency
options.why: Working from the narrowest, fastest signal outward finds the direct cause quickly and, if that is inconclusive, widens to catch a dependency that failed first and took the service down with it.

options.text: `journalctl -p err -b` first, since severity filtering always finds the root cause fastest regardless of scope
options.why: Starting with a system-wide severity filter skips the fastest, most direct signal — the unit's own status and its own log entries — which usually explains the failure on its own.

options.text: `journalctl -u <unit> -f` first, to watch it fail live before checking anything else — following live only helps while reproducing the failure in real time; the described scenario is investigating a failure that has already occurred, for which status and boot logs come first
options.why: Following live only helps while reproducing the failure in real time; the described scenario is investigating a failure that has already occurred, for which status and boot logs come first.

options.text: `journalctl -p err -b` alone is sufficient and the other two commands add nothing useful
options.why: A severity-wide filter can miss a failure logged at a lower severity or buried among many other units' errors; the unit-specific commands narrow the search far more directly.

items.rationale: `systemctl status <unit>` gives the fastest read — the last few lines and exit status. `journalctl -u` narrowed to the unit and `journalctl -b` narrowed to this boot together widen to everything that unit logged this boot. `journalctl -p err` widens further still, to catch a dependency that failed first and is the real cause; `journalctl -f` is the live-following variant used while reproducing a fault in real time.

items.stem: A huge log file is deleted by hand to free disk space, but `df -h` still reports the filesystem as full afterward. Why, and what is the correct long-term fix?

options.text: The daemon still has the file open, so its blocks stay allocated until the descriptor closes; the fix is scheduled log rotation, not manual deletion
options.why: Deleting a file a process still holds open frees no space until that process closes or restarts, and rotation is what avoids ever needing manual deletion again.

options.text: `df -h` is simply slow to update and will reflect the freed space after a short wait
options.why: The reported figure will not change on its own; the blocks remain allocated as long as the daemon keeps the deleted file's descriptor open, however long that is.

options.text: The log must actually be compressed already, which is why deleting it did not free space
options.why: Compression status has nothing to do with whether deleting the file frees its blocks; the cause here is an open file descriptor held by a running process.

options.text: The filesystem must have run out of inodes rather than blocks — inode exhaustion produces a distinct "No space left" symptom with free blocks still showing; this scenario describes blocks that remain allocated, consistent with a held-open deleted file
options.why: Inode exhaustion produces a distinct "No space left" symptom with free blocks still showing; this scenario describes blocks that remain allocated, consistent with a held-open deleted file.

items.rationale: Removing a file a daemon still has open frees no space at all until that descriptor closes, which is exactly the `df`/`du` discrepancy this concept explains. The durable fix is configuring log rotation so files never grow unbounded in the first place, rather than deleting a huge log after the fact.

items.stem: A daemon cannot be signalled to reopen its log file after rotation, but the log still must not grow unbounded. Which `logrotate` directive fits, and what is its cost?

options.text: `copytruncate`, which copies the log aside and truncates the original in place — at the cost of losing whatever is written between the copy and the truncate
options.why: Copying then truncating keeps the daemon writing to the same inode without needing to signal it, but there is a small window where in-flight writes can be lost.

options.text: `postrotate`, since it is the directive used whenever a daemon cannot be signalled — a `postrotate` script is exactly the mechanism used to signal a daemon; it is the wrong choice for a daemon that specifically cannot be signalled
options.why: A `postrotate` script is exactly the mechanism used to signal a daemon; it is the wrong choice for a daemon that specifically cannot be signalled.

options.text: `compress`, since compressing the rotated file avoids needing to signal the daemon at all
options.why: Compression controls whether old generations are stored compressed; it has no bearing on whether the daemon needs to be told to reopen its log file.

options.text: `delaycompress`, which defers the problem to the next rotation cycle instead of solving it
options.why: Deferred compression changes when compression happens, not whether the daemon's open file descriptor is handled; it does not address the stated problem at all.

items.rationale: `copytruncate` copies the log's contents aside and truncates the original file in place, so a daemon that cannot be signalled keeps writing to the same inode without interruption — at the cost of losing anything written in the brief window between the copy and the truncate.

items.stem: Put the five stages of the boot process in order, from power-on to a running system.

options.text: Firmware, bootloader, kernel plus initramfs, PID 1 (the init system), then units until the default target
options.why: Each stage hands control to the next: firmware finds a boot device, the bootloader loads the kernel, the kernel mounts the real root, and the init system brings up the rest.

options.text: Bootloader, firmware, kernel, units, then PID 1 — this ordering has the first two stages reversed
options.why: Firmware runs first, before any bootloader can be found or executed — this ordering has the first two stages reversed.

options.text: Firmware, kernel, bootloader, PID 1, then units — the kernel cannot be loaded until the bootloader has found and loaded it into memory
options.why: The bootloader runs before the kernel, not after it — the kernel cannot be loaded until the bootloader has found and loaded it into memory.

options.text: Firmware, bootloader, PID 1, kernel, then units
options.why: PID 1 cannot start before the kernel does, since the kernel is what starts PID 1 in the first place — the third and fourth stages are swapped here.

items.rationale: The ordered handover is: firmware initialises hardware and finds a boot device; the bootloader loads the kernel and an initramfs; the kernel initialises and mounts the real root filesystem; it starts PID 1; and the init system activates units until the default target is reached.

items.stem: `systemd-analyze blame` names a unit that took 30 seconds during a slow boot, but nothing else was waiting on that unit while it ran. Was it the cause of the slow boot?

options.text: Not necessarily — `blame` measures duration, not delay, and a unit that runs in parallel with nothing waiting on it costs nothing to boot time
options.why: Because activation happens in parallel wherever dependencies allow, a slow unit only actually delays boot if something else is blocked waiting for it to finish.

options.text: Yes, the slowest-duration unit in `blame`'s output is always what held boot up
options.why: Duration alone does not establish delay when units run in parallel; `systemd-analyze critical-chain` is what shows the ordering chain that actually determined boot time.

options.text: No, because `blame` only reports on the firmware phase, which happens before Linux is even running
options.why: `blame` reports on userspace unit initialisation time, not the firmware phase, which happens before anything on the disk is running at all.

options.text: No, but only because the unit must have failed rather than merely run slowly — nothing in the scenario suggests the unit failed; it ran successfully but slowly, and the question is whether that slowness delayed anything else
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests the unit failed; it ran successfully but slowly, and the question is whether that slowness delayed anything else.

items.rationale: systemd activates units in parallel wherever the dependency graph allows, so `blame`'s ranking by duration does not by itself show what delayed boot. `systemd-analyze critical-chain` identifies the actual ordering chain that determined when boot converged, which a merely slow but unwaited-on unit does not appear on.

items.stem: Name three capabilities UEFI provides that legacy BIOS does not.

options.text: An EFI System Partition holding bootloaders as files, GPT partitioning supporting disks beyond roughly 2 TiB, and Secure Boot
options.why: Each is a direct consequence of UEFI reading filesystems and executables rather than a fixed 512-byte boot sector the way legacy BIOS does.

options.text: Faster boot times, larger RAM support, and multi-core CPU support — none of those are properties that distinguish UEFI from BIOS; the genuine distinguishing capabilities are the EFI System Partition, GPT support, and Secure Boot
options.why: None of those are properties that distinguish UEFI from BIOS; the genuine distinguishing capabilities are the EFI System Partition, GPT support, and Secure Boot.

options.text: GRUB as the bootloader, kernel parameter passing, and the initramfs
options.why: GRUB, kernel parameters and the initramfs are all present regardless of which firmware generation is in use; they are not UEFI-specific capabilities.

options.text: Support for more than four partitions total, journaling filesystems, and disk encryption
options.why: Journaling and disk encryption are filesystem-level features unrelated to firmware; only the partition-count and disk-size limits are the genuine BIOS-versus-UEFI distinction here.

items.rationale: UEFI understands filesystems and reads an EFI executable from a dedicated FAT-formatted EFI System Partition rather than executing a 512-byte boot sector. That capability is what enables GPT partitioning (removing MBR's four-partition and roughly 2 TiB limits) and Secure Boot, none of which legacy BIOS provides.

items.stem: An administrator disables Secure Boot in firmware settings to load an unsigned kernel module, and the machine continues to boot normally afterward using UEFI. Is that expected?

options.text: Yes — Secure Boot is one optional UEFI feature, and turning it off does not disable UEFI booting itself
options.why: UEFI and Secure Boot are not the same thing; Secure Boot can be switched off independently while the firmware continues to boot through its normal UEFI path.

options.text: No, disabling Secure Boot should force the machine to fall back to legacy BIOS booting
options.why: Secure Boot is a UEFI feature layered on top of the normal boot path; disabling it does not revert the firmware to an entirely different, older boot mode.

options.text: No, because Secure Boot is required for the EFI System Partition to be readable at all
options.why: The EFI System Partition is read as part of ordinary UEFI booting regardless of whether Secure Boot's signature verification is enabled.

options.text: Yes, but only because GRUB itself disables Secure Boot automatically when an unsigned module is present
options.why: GRUB does not silently disable a firmware-level setting; Secure Boot was turned off directly in firmware, which is what allowed the unsigned module to load.

items.rationale: Secure Boot is one optional UEFI feature that verifies the signature of each executable in the boot chain; it is not synonymous with UEFI itself. Turning it off to permit an unsigned kernel module leaves UEFI booting — the EFI System Partition, GPT, everything else — unaffected.

items.stem: An administrator edits `/etc/default/grub` to change the default boot entry and reboots, but the change has no effect. What step was skipped?

options.text: Regenerating `grub.cfg` — with `update-grub` on Debian-family systems, or `grub2-mkconfig` on Red Hat-family ones — since `/etc/default/grub` only feeds that generation step
options.why: `grub.cfg` is the file GRUB actually reads at boot, and it is generated from `/etc/default/grub` rather than being read directly, so a source edit alone has no effect until regeneration runs.

options.text: Nothing was skipped; `/etc/default/grub` is read directly by GRUB at boot time
options.why: GRUB reads the generated `grub.cfg`, not `/etc/default/grub` directly — the source file only takes effect once the generation step rewrites the config GRUB actually loads.

options.text: The change needed `systemctl daemon-reload` to take effect — `daemon-reload` re-reads systemd unit files and has nothing to do with GRUB's configuration, which is generated by a separate, unrelated tool
options.why: `daemon-reload` re-reads systemd unit files and has nothing to do with GRUB's configuration, which is generated by a separate, unrelated tool.

options.text: UEFI Secure Boot must be blocking the new default entry from being honoured
options.why: Secure Boot verifies signatures on boot executables; it does not selectively block a default-entry change, and nothing in the scenario points at signature verification.

items.rationale: GRUB's runtime configuration, `grub.cfg`, is generated from `/etc/default/grub` and the scripts in `/etc/grub.d/`, not edited directly — the same "edited the source, did not rebuild the artefact" shape as a systemd unit needing `daemon-reload`. `update-grub` (Debian-family) or `grub2-mkconfig` (Red Hat-family) must run to regenerate it.

items.stem: An administrator on a Red Hat-family server runs `update-grub` to regenerate the configuration after a kernel update, and it fails: command not found. Why?

options.text: `update-grub` is a Debian-family wrapper script; Red Hat-family systems regenerate the configuration with `grub2-mkconfig` instead
options.why: The two families use different commands for the same underlying operation, and reaching for the Debian-family one on a Red Hat-family system is exactly the family mix-up this concept tests.

options.text: GRUB configuration regeneration is not supported at all on Red Hat-family systems
options.why: Regeneration is fully supported; it simply uses a different command name, `grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg`, on that family.

options.text: The command failed because Secure Boot is enabled and blocking configuration regeneration
options.why: Secure Boot governs signature verification of boot executables and has no bearing on whether a configuration-generation command exists on the system.

options.text: The command failed because the kernel update has not finished installing yet — the failure described is "command not found," which indicates the wrong tool was invoked, not that an install is still in progress
options.why: The failure described is "command not found," which indicates the wrong tool was invoked, not that an install is still in progress.

items.rationale: `update-grub` is a Debian-family wrapper around `grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg`, and it does not exist on Red Hat-family systems, which instead call `grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` directly — reaching for the wrong family's command is a mix-up the exam can present directly.

items.stem: A kernel package was installed an hour ago. What does `uname -r` report right now, and when does that change?

options.text: The previously running kernel version — installing a package changes what is on disk, not what is running, until the machine reboots
options.why: The newly installed kernel takes effect only after a reboot; until then the running kernel, and therefore `uname -r`'s output, is whatever was booted before the install.

options.text: The newly installed kernel version, since installation immediately updates the running kernel
options.why: Installing a kernel package changes files under `/boot` and `/lib/modules`; it does not swap the kernel actually running in memory until the next reboot.

options.text: The distribution release rather than any kernel version, since `uname -r` reports OS release information
options.why: `uname -r` reports the kernel release specifically; the distribution release is reported separately by `/etc/os-release`.

options.text: An error, since two kernel versions cannot coexist on disk at the same time — each has its own image and module directory, selectable from the bootloader menu
options.why: Multiple kernel versions coexisting on disk is normal and expected — each has its own image and module directory, selectable from the bootloader menu.

items.rationale: Installing a kernel package changes what is on disk — a new image under `/boot` and new modules under `/lib/modules/<version>/` — but not what is currently running. `uname -r` continues to report the previously booted kernel until the machine actually reboots into the new one.

items.stem: A server does not come back after a kernel upgrade and reboot: the GRUB menu appears and the kernel prints messages before the process stops, with no login prompt ever appearing. Which stage does that narrow the fault to?

options.text: After the kernel starts and before the init system finishes — the initramfs, the root filesystem, or a failing unit, rather than firmware or the bootloader
options.why: Because the GRUB menu and kernel messages both appeared successfully, firmware and the bootloader are ruled out, leaving the stages between kernel start and a completed boot.

options.text: Firmware or the bootloader, since any boot failure should be treated as a firmware problem first
options.why: The GRUB menu appearing and the kernel printing messages both demonstrate firmware and the bootloader worked correctly; the fault lies later in the sequence.

options.text: The package manager's database, since a kernel upgrade updates package metadata
options.why: A corrupted package database would not produce this specific symptom of the kernel printing messages and then stopping before a login prompt.

options.text: UEFI Secure Boot, since an upgraded kernel is unsigned by default — a Secure Boot signature failure would typically prevent the kernel from starting at all, not let it print messages and then stall partway through initialisation
options.why: A Secure Boot signature failure would typically prevent the kernel from starting at all, not let it print messages and then stall partway through initialisation.

items.rationale: Knowing the stage order makes a boot failure diagnosable: the GRUB menu appearing rules out firmware and the bootloader, and kernel messages appearing before a stall rules out the kernel failing to start at all, narrowing the fault to the initramfs, the root filesystem, or an init-system unit — after which selecting the previous kernel is the standard first recovery step.
